topic_title: E-Filing Portal Failures and the Limitation Clock at NCLT/NCLAT: What the Law Actually Excuses
angle: A guide for IBC litigants and counsel on when a tribunal's own e-filing system failure can be used to seek exclusion of time from the limitation period for an appeal or application, and the limits of that relief given NCLAT's 45-day outer cap under Section 61(2).
key_points: NCLAT's appeal limitation under Section 61(2) of the IBC is 30 days, extendable by a further 15 days on sufficient cause, with the Supreme Court having held NCLAT has no inherent power to condone delay beyond that 45-day outer limit

The Supreme Court has nonetheless held that where a litigant makes a bona fide, timely attempt to e-file before the deadline but is prevented by a tribunal's own backend/portal technical glitch, the period the portal was non-functional can be excluded from the limitation computation rather than treated as part of the delay to be condoned
The operative principle invoked is actus curiae neminem gravabit — an act (or failure) of the court/tribunal itself should not prejudice a litigant who acted diligently

Practical evidentiary steps: preserving screenshots/error logs of failed OTP or upload attempts, timestamps, and promptly seeking a report from the tribunal's own registry confirming the system issue, since courts have relied on exactly such a registry report to grant relief
This exclusion-of-time route is distinct from, and does not override, the separate question of whether sufficient cause exists to condone any further, unrelated delay within the 45-day window
The same reasoning has been applied to e-filing failures in income-tax appellate and other tribunal contexts, so the principle is not confined to IBC appeals
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: confirmed: NCLAT appeal limitation under IBC Section 61(2) is 30 days plus a further 15 days on sufficient cause, a 45-day outer limit NCLAT cannot extend on equitable grounds (Supreme Court authority)

confirmed: in Regional Provident Fund Commissioner-II v. Ms. Mamta Binani & Ors. (2026 INSC 1003), the Supreme Court held a tribunal e-filing portal's backend failure on the last day of limitation could be excluded from the limitation period rather than count against the litigant, remitting the matter for NCLAT to decide residual sufficient cause
confirmed: the Court relied on a registry-submitted report confirming the portal's technical failure as key evidence

topic_title: Revoking a Granted Patent in India: Section 64 Revocation Petitions Explained
angle: A guide for a competitor or any 'person interested' seeking to invalidate an already-granted Indian patent, covering who can file, the forum, the statutory grounds, and how a revocation petition differs from pre/post-grant opposition and from a revocation counterclaim in an infringement suit.
key_points: Under Section 64(1) of the Patents Act, 1970, a patent may be revoked on a petition by 'any person interested' or by the Central Government, or on a counterclaim by a defendant in an infringement suit
Since the IP Appellate Board's abolition in 2021, standalone revocation petitions are filed before the jurisdictional High Court rather than a specialised tribunal
Where revocation is raised as a counterclaim in an infringement suit filed in a District Court, Section 104 requires the suit together with the counterclaim to be transferred to the High Court
A person interested who could pursue either route (standalone petition or counterclaim) has a statutory right to choose, and that choice cannot be forced by the opposing party

Statutory grounds under Section 64(1) include prior claiming by another Indian patent with an earlier priority date, grant to a person not entitled to apply, wrongful obtaining in contravention of the petitioner's own rights, lack of novelty or inventive step, insufficiency of disclosure, and non-compliance with disclosure/working requirements

Revocation is distinct from pre-grant opposition (Section 25(1), before grant) and post-grant opposition (Section 25(2), within 12 months of grant) — a revocation petition can be filed at any time after grant and after the opposition window has closed, and is the only route once a patent is already granted and unopposed
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: confirmed: Section 64(1) revocation can be sought by a person interested, the Central Government, or by counterclaim in an infringement suit
confirmed: post-IPAB abolition (2021), standalone revocation petitions now go to the High Court
confirmed: Section 104 requires transfer of an infringement suit with a revocation counterclaim to the High Court

note: exact current statutory text of all Section 64(1) grounds (a) through to the later sub-clauses should be verified against the Patents Act before publication, since some secondary sources still reference the since-abolished Appellate Board as a forum

topic_title: Can a Builder Cancel Your Allotment and Forfeit Your Payment? RERA's Limits on Forfeiture Clauses
angle: A guide for homebuyers facing allotment cancellation (for alleged default on instalments) or who want to withdraw from a project themselves, on how RERA authorities have capped how much of the paid amount a builder can actually forfeit, regardless of what the builder-buyer agreement says.
key_points: Several state RERA authorities have held that a builder-buyer agreement clause allowing forfeiture of a large percentage (commonly 20% or more) of the sale consideration or paid amount as 'earnest money' is liable to be read down as a one-sided, unconscionable term under the RERA framework

Haryana RERA has capped forfeiture at 10% of the sale/unit consideration in both builder-initiated cancellations for buyer default and buyer-initiated withdrawals, treating any contrary clause as void, and has applied the same cap even to commercial unit cancellations
MahaRERA has taken an even stricter line in some orders, capping forfeiture at 2% for homebuyer-initiated cancellations, and has applied this retroactively to already-registered projects

The underlying consumer-law principle (invoked alongside RERA) is that an unreasonably high forfeiture clause amounts to a penalty rather than genuine pre-estimated liquidated damages, and the Supreme Court has limited builders' ability to forfeit earnest money on this basis in consumer/contract disputes (e.g. the Godrej Projects Development line of cases)

A buyer facing a cancellation notice or a builder refusing to refund beyond a deducted percentage should check the applicable state RERA's specific orders/circulars on forfeiture caps, since there is no single uniform national percentage — Haryana and Maharashtra positions differ
Remedy: a buyer can file a RERA complaint seeking refund of the amount withheld beyond the authority's recognised cap, with interest, rather than accepting the agreement's forfeiture clause as final
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: confirmed: Haryana RERA has held forfeiture cannot exceed 10% of sale consideration, voiding contrary clauses, in both builder-cancellation and buyer-withdrawal scenarios
confirmed: MahaRERA orders have capped homebuyer-cancellation forfeiture at 2%, applied retroactively to registered projects

note: there is no single pan-India statutory forfeiture percentage under RERA itself — the caps described are authority-specific orders/practice, which should be described as such rather than as a uniform rule, and the Godrej Projects Development v. Anil Karlekar Supreme Court outcome should be confirmed against the final judgment before citing its holding

topic_title: Price Support Scheme vs Market Intervention Scheme: How Farmers of Perishable Crops Get Price Protection Without an MSP
angle: A guide for farmers and FPOs growing crops that have no announced Minimum Support Price (fruits, vegetables, onions, tomatoes, potatoes) on how the Market Intervention Scheme and the related Price Support Scheme and Price Deficiency Payment Scheme under PM-AASHA actually work, who triggers them, and how a farmer accesses the benefit.
key_points: PM-AASHA (Pradhan Mantri Annadata Aay Sanrakshan Abhiyan) is the umbrella scheme with three components: Price Support Scheme (PSS), Price Deficiency Payment Scheme (PDPS), and Market Intervention Scheme (MIS)
PSS applies only to crops with an announced MSP that lack one (oilseeds, pulses, copra) and involves direct government procurement at MSP from registered farmers when market prices fall below it

MIS is specifically for perishable horticultural/agricultural produce that has no announced MSP at all (e.g. onions, tomatoes, potatoes) and is implemented only on a specific request from the concerned state/UT government, not automatically

MIS procurement is typically triggered when there is at least a 10% fall in market prices compared to the previous normal season, with losses shared between the Centre and the state (commonly on a 50:50 basis, higher for North-Eastern states), subject to a pre-approved quantity ceiling

A 2025 revision allows states to instead pay farmers the difference between the Market Intervention Price and the actual selling price directly into their bank accounts, rather than physical procurement

A farmer/FPO seeking MIS benefit should approach the state agriculture/horticulture department (which requests Central approval) rather than a Central government agency directly, since MIS is state-request-driven, unlike PSS procurement
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: confirmed: MIS covers perishable produce without an announced MSP and operates on state/UT request, cost-shared with the Centre
confirmed: PSS covers oilseeds/pulses/copra procurement at MSP when market price falls below it

note: the exact current cost-sharing ratio, the price-fall trigger percentage, and the procurement quantity ceiling should be re-confirmed against the latest PM-AASHA/MIS guidelines in force at time of writing, since these parameters are revised periodically

topic_title: Look Out Circulars Against Loan Defaulters: When Can a Bank Actually Stop You Leaving India?
angle: A guide for guarantors and borrowers facing a bank-initiated Look Out Circular (LOC) on how LOCs are supposed to work, why banks use them as an informal recovery tool, and how to get one lifted — especially once the underlying debt has been settled or resolved.
key_points: An LOC is issued by the Bureau of Immigration on a request from an authorised agency; for public sector banks, RBI/government instructions have at various points allowed LOC requests in large wilful-defaulter cases, but courts have repeatedly stressed it is not a routine debt-recovery tool

Courts have held that a bank's own internal letter or request cannot by itself operate as 'law' restricting the fundamental right to travel abroad under Article 21 — there must be a proper legal basis and due process

An LOC issued against a guarantor or borrower does not automatically lapse when the underlying loan account is closed (e.g. via a resolution plan or settlement) — it has to be affirmatively recalled, so borrowers should specifically seek its recall as part of any settlement/closure, not assume it disappears

Courts have expressed concern that extending LOC powers loosely to bank debt recovery could invite private creditors/NBFCs to seek similar restraints, so judicial scrutiny of the basis for an LOC is relatively strict

Practical route to challenge: a writ petition before the jurisdictional High Court seeking quashing of the LOC, placing on record proof that the underlying debt is closed/settled and that no other proceeding justifies the restraint
Distinguish an LOC from a court-ordered travel restraint (e.g. in execution or contempt proceedings) — the legal basis and challenge route differ
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: confirmed: courts have held a bank's letter to the Bureau of Immigration is not 'law' and cannot restrict the Article 21 right to travel merely on that basis (Madras High Court, Kondepati Ganga Prasad v. Bank of Baroda, Oct 2026)

note: the precise government/RBI framework governing which categories of bank dues justify an LOC request has been revised over time (various Ministry of Finance/Home Affairs office memoranda) — the current applicable circular and its exact monetary/wilful-defaulter thresholds should be confirmed before publication rather than stated as a fixed figure

topic_title: Your Trademark Lapsed Years Ago — Can You Still Get It Back? The Registry's Form O-3 Notice Requirement
angle: A guide for proprietors of a trademark the Registry has removed from the register for non-renewal, explaining the mandatory Form O-3 expiry-notice procedure under Section 25 of the Trade Marks Act and how a defective or unproven notice can let a proprietor revive even a decades-lapsed mark.
key_points: Before removing a mark from the register for non-renewal, the Registry is required to send a notice (Form O-3) of the upcoming expiry, giving the proprietor an opportunity to renew
Courts have consistently held this notice requirement is mandatory, not merely directory — a mark cannot be validly removed without it (Union of India v. Malhotra Book Depot line of authority)

An internal Registry dispatch log, by itself, has been held insufficient to prove the notice was actually sent to or received by the proprietor — the Registry must produce reliable evidence of actual dispatch/receipt

Where the Registry cannot prove compliance, courts have permitted the proprietor to file a fresh renewal application (on payment of the prescribed fee) even decades after the purported lapse — one 2026 Delhi High Court case revived a mark after a roughly 26-year gap

Practical steps for a proprietor: request the Registry's complete file/correspondence record for the mark, check whether a Form O-3 notice was actually issued (not just logged) and to the then-current registered address, and file a writ petition if the Registry relies only on an internal system entry

This is a narrow, document-driven remedy — it does not help where the Registry can actually prove the notice was sent and received; practitioners should caution that reviving a long-lapsed mark may also face third-party rights that accrued in the interim
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: confirmed: Form O-3 notice before removal for non-renewal is a mandatory procedural requirement under the Trade Marks Act/Rules, per settled Delhi High Court authority
confirmed: an internal dispatch log alone has been held insufficient proof of actual dispatch/receipt (Delhi HC, Punam Chand Kedia re: 'HMP' mark, Sept 2026)
note: exact rule number for Form O-3 under the Trade Marks Rules, 2017 (as amended) should be verified against the current Rules before publication

topic_title: Can a Bank Be Penalised for Not Complying With a Garnishee Order? When 'Inoperative Account' and Similar Defences Work
angle: A guide distinct from ordinary decree-execution garnishee proceedings, focused specifically on when a bank can resist, or avoid being branded a defaulter over, a statutory recovery garnishee order (e.g. from EPFO, ESI, or a tax recovery officer) issued against a customer's account.
key_points: A garnishee/attachment order directed at a bank requires the bank to pay over funds in the named account to the recovery officer — but the bank's obligation is limited to what the account actually and lawfully holds at the relevant time

Courts have quashed 'deemed defaulter' findings against a bank where the targeted account was factually inoperative, frozen, or otherwise unable to be operated — the recovery officer must verify the account's actual status before escalating non-compliance against the bank itself

A bank facing a garnishee order over an account it has itself frozen (e.g. on fraud/money-mule suspicion) is in a different position from one simply refusing to pay from a functioning account — courts scrutinise the reason for non-payment closely
Natural justice requires giving the bank a genuine opportunity to explain non-compliance before it is branded a defaulter, rather than a mechanical escalation

This is distinct from Order XXI CPC garnishee proceedings by an ordinary decree-holder against a judgment-debtor's bank account, which follow a separate civil-procedure framework with their own defences (the bank is a third party there too, but the statutory scheme differs from a tax/statutory-dues recovery garnishee)

Practical note for banks and customers alike: document the account's operative status and any freeze/restriction at the time the garnishee order is served, since that record is the key evidence in any later challenge
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: confirmed: Calcutta High Court quashed ESI garnishee orders against SBI and a 'deemed defaulter' finding where the targeted account was inoperative, holding the finding was made without application of mind and violated natural justice (Oct 2026)

note: this guide should clearly flag for readers that it covers statutory-recovery garnishee orders (EPFO/ESI/tax authorities), not Order XXI CPC civil-decree garnishee proceedings, which the site's existing 'Execution of a Money Decree and Garnishee Proceedings' guide already covers

topic_title: FSSAI Licensing for Slaughterhouses and Meat Processing Units: Why 'Registration' Isn't Enough Above a Small Capacity
angle: A compliance guide for abattoir and meat-processing operators on why the FSSAI's lighter-touch 'registration' route (meant for petty food businesses) is capacity-capped specifically for slaughtering activity, and when a full/regular licence becomes mandatory regardless of turnover.
key_points: FSSAI's three-tier structure (registration / state licence / central licence) is generally turnover-based, but slaughtering and meat-processing activity is treated differently: the 'petty' registration route for slaughtering is capped by daily slaughtering capacity (a small number of large/small animals or poultry per day), not simply by annual turnover

A slaughterhouse operating above that daily-capacity threshold needs a full/regular FSSAI licence even if its overall turnover would otherwise qualify it for the cheaper registration route — a registration certificate does not authorise large-scale slaughtering

Courts have upheld enforcement action (closure/penalty) against operators who continued large-scale slaughtering on the strength of a mere registration certificate, rejecting arguments that registration was an adequate stop-gap (Allahabad High Court, Sept 2026)

Meat Processing and Slaughtering Houses are typically listed as a distinct category in FSSAI's licensing fee schedule, separate from general food manufacturing, reflecting this capacity-based (not purely turnover-based) treatment

Practical compliance step: an operator planning to scale up slaughtering capacity should apply for the full licence before crossing the capacity threshold, not after, since operating above it without a licence exposes the business to closure and prosecution, not just a penalty
This sits alongside, and should be read together with, general FSSAI licensing obligations for any food business operator
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: confirmed: Allahabad High Court held a large-scale slaughterhouse needs a regular FSSAI licence and that a petty-business registration certificate is not sufficient, dismissing a challenge to enforcement action (Sept 2026)

note: the exact current daily-capacity figures defining the 'petty' slaughtering threshold (number of large/small animals or poultry per day) vary across secondary sources and should be confirmed against the current FSSAI Licensing and Registration Regulations before publication rather than stated as a fixed number

topic_title: How the CCI Proves a Cartel: Bid-Rigging, Circumstantial Evidence and the Section 3(3) Presumption
angle: A guide for businesses facing a CCI cartel/bid-rigging investigation (or advising clients who are) on how the burden of proof actually works under Section 3(3) of the Competition Act, what kind of circumstantial evidence the CCI relies on in the absence of a written agreement, and what a successful rebuttal looks like.
key_points: Section 3(3) of the Competition Act creates agreements between competitors in four categories (including bid-rigging/collusive bidding) presumed to cause an appreciable adverse effect on competition (AAEC) once the CCI establishes the agreement exists

The burden is two-staged: the CCI/Director General must first establish the existence of the agreement or concerted practice; only once that is shown does the burden shift to the parties to rebut the presumption of AAEC

Because cartels are typically concealed, the CCI relies heavily on circumstantial evidence where no written agreement exists — commonly cited indicators include near-identical bid pricing despite differing cost structures, common patterns in bid submission (e.g. shared visitor-register entries at a tender office), and communication trails suggesting prior coordination

The Competition Act does not prescribe a 'beyond reasonable doubt' criminal standard — cartel contraventions are treated as a civil wrong, and the CCI's own decisional practice has developed what counts as sufficient circumstantial proof

A rebuttal that merely denies coordination without addressing the specific circumstantial indicators the DG/CCI relied on is unlikely to succeed — successful rebuttals typically show an independent, non-collusive explanation for the pricing/bidding pattern (e.g. genuine common input costs)

Liability can attach differently up and down a distribution chain — in some CCI orders, only authorised dealers/resellers who actually exchanged bid information were penalised while the principal manufacturer was exonerated for lack of evidence of its own involvement, while in others the principal itself has been penalised directly for cartel conduct
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: confirmed: Section 3(3) creates a presumption of AAEC for specified categories of horizontal agreement including bid-rigging, rebuttable by the parties once the CCI establishes the agreement's existence
confirmed: CCI has relied on circumstantial evidence (matching bid prices, shared visitor-register entries) in bid-rigging cases absent a written agreement
note: whether a particular manufacturer/principal is held liable alongside dealers depends on case-specific evidence of its involvement — this varies by case and should not be stated as a fixed rule

topic_title: Your Company's 'POSH Appellate Committee' May Be Illegal: What Section 18 and Rule 11 Actually Require
angle: A compliance guide for employers who have set up, or are considering setting up, an internal appellate body to hear appeals from an Internal Committee's POSH findings, explaining why courts have held employers cannot simply invent their own appellate authority, and what the correct appellate route actually is.
key_points: Section 18 of the POSH Act gives a person aggrieved by an Internal Committee's recommendations a right of appeal within 90 days, but the Act itself does not let the employer design its own appellate body

Rule 11 of the POSH Rules points to the appellate authority as whatever is provided under the employer's applicable service rules; where no service rules apply, the fallback is the authority notified under the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946

Courts have held that a combined reading of Section 18 and Rule 11 gives an employer no authority or jurisdiction to constitute its own, self-styled 'Appellate Authority' — doing so can taint the entire disciplinary process that follows and lead to any resulting penalty being quashed in its entirety (Bombay High Court, Ashok Upadhyay v. Union Bank of India, Aug 2026)

Employers should first check (a) whether applicable service rules already designate an appellate authority, and (b) whether the state government has notified an authority under the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act for establishments of the relevant size — rather than appointing an internal panel or committee of their own choosing
Where no authority has actually been notified for a given establishment, affected parties have been left to approach the jurisdictional High Court by writ petition as the practical route of appeal

Practical audit step: every employer's POSH policy should be checked against this framework now, before an appeal is ever filed, since discovering the appellate route was invalid only after a penalty has been imposed and challenged is far costlier to fix
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: confirmed: Bombay High Court held Section 18 read with Rule 11 gives an employer no power to create its own Appellate Authority, quashing a penalty for that reason (Aug 2026)

note: the exact employee-count threshold for notification of a Standing-Orders appellate authority, and whether a given state has actually notified one, varies and should be checked against the specific state's notification rather than assumed uniform

topic_title: Force Majeure Extensions in NHAI Concession Agreements: How a 'Cure Period' Actually Gets Added to Your Concession Term
angle: A guide for highway concessionaires and their advisors on how a force majeure event (illustrated by COVID-19 toll suspensions) translates into an actual extension of the concession period, what a concessionaire needs to prove, and why a prior settlement of a related claim can block relitigating it later.
key_points: Most NHAI concession/BOT agreements provide that a force majeure event excusing the concessionaire's performance also entitles it to an extension of the concession period for the duration the event actually disrupted operations/revenue

The extension claimed is not automatically whatever the concessionaire requests — tribunals have drawn a distinction between full toll-suspension days (clearly compensable) and days of merely 'severely depressed' toll collection (also found compensable where proved), with NHAI sometimes granting only the clearer, shorter period administratively and leaving the balance to be fought out in arbitration

A settlement agreement recorded during the concession's life that resolves a specific claim (e.g. de-scoping of certain works) closes that issue for good — a party cannot later dress up the same resolved claim as a fresh counterclaim in a subsequent arbitration over an unrelated extension dispute

Challenges to an arbitral award granting such an extension face the ordinary, narrow Section 34 standard — a court will not interfere merely because it would have read the concession/settlement documents differently, so long as the tribunal's interpretation was a plausible one

Practical evidentiary point for concessionaires: contemporaneous toll-collection data showing the extent of depression during the claimed disruption period is central to proving entitlement beyond the undisputed suspension days

This sits alongside broader 'force majeure in infrastructure contracts' guidance already on the site, but focuses specifically on how such claims interact with a concession's extension mechanism and with prior settlements of related claims
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: confirmed: Delhi High Court upheld an arbitral award granting a 53-day concession extension (25 days full suspension + 28 days depressed collection) to a BOT concessionaire for COVID-19 disruption, and rejected NHAI's related counterclaim as already resolved by an earlier settlement (July 2026, Nagpur-Kondhali NH-6 concession)

note: exact force-majeure/extension clause wording varies by concession agreement vintage and model (BOT vs HAM) — this guide should describe the general mechanism rather than quote one agreement's specific clause as universal

topic_title: Can a RERA Order Be Reopened After It's Final? Review Applications and Fraud Discovered During Execution
angle: A guide for homebuyers (and developers) on the limited circumstances in which a RERA authority can revisit its own earlier, final order — particularly where fraud or concealment by a party only comes to light after execution proceedings have already begun.
key_points: A RERA authority's order ordinarily becomes final and executable after the statutory period for appeal/compliance lapses, and is not open to being reopened on a mere second look

Where a complainant discovers during execution that the respondent concealed material facts from the authority during the original proceedings — such as having already sold the same unit to third parties while the original complaint was pending — RERA authorities have treated this as a proper basis to revisit the earlier order on review, rather than treating the order as closed

A review on this basis can change the nature of the relief itself — an order originally directing possession can be converted into a refund-with-interest order where possession is no longer achievable because of the respondent's own concealed conduct

A party's deliberate absence from the original proceedings (rather than genuine lack of notice) does not insulate it from this kind of review once concealment is discovered — if anything, courts/authorities treat staying away while concealing facts as an aggravating factor

Separately from refund, a developer found to have created third-party rights over a unit already subject to a regulatory direction can face an independent penalty for that conduct, on top of whatever relief is given to the original complainant

Practical tip for buyers sitting on an old, unenforced possession order: check the property's current ownership/registration records before assuming the order remains capable of being executed as possession, since years of non-enforcement can mean the unit has quietly changed hands
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: confirmed: MahaRERA converted an original possession order into a refund-with-interest order, plus a separate penalty on the developer, after the buyer discovered during execution that the developer (who had stayed absent from the original proceedings) had already sold the unit to third parties (review order reported July 2026)

note: the statutory/regulatory basis for a RERA authority's review power (as opposed to an appeal to the Appellate Tribunal) varies by state RERA rules and should be confirmed against the applicable state's RERA regulations before publication

topic_title: Suing for Specific Performance and the Seller Resold the Property? How Courts Secure the Sale Price Pending Trial
angle: A practical guide for a specific-performance plaintiff who discovers, mid-suit, that the defendant-seller has sold the disputed property to a third party, on the interim relief available to secure the money at stake while the suit over title/performance continues.
key_points: Where a seller sells the suit property to a third party after a specific-performance suit is filed, the doctrine of lis pendens (Section 52, Transfer of Property Act) means the subsequent buyer takes subject to the outcome of the pending suit — but that alone does not guarantee the original plaintiff gets the property back if specific performance is ultimately refused

Courts have used their interim injunction powers to maintain status quo over the property itself (preventing further alienation or change) while a specific-performance suit is pending, even after a subsequent sale has already occurred

Separately, where there is a risk the seller may dissipate or place beyond reach the sale proceeds received from the subsequent (second) sale, courts have directed the seller to deposit a substantial sum in court — effectively securing the monetary stake — pending final adjudication, without that direction amounting to a final finding on entitlement

Such an interim deposit order is explicitly made on a prima facie basis and does not predetermine whether the original plaintiff will ultimately get specific performance, restitution of the deposited sum, or damages — it simply preserves the fund so that whichever remedy is eventually granted is not rendered illusory

Practical steps for a plaintiff in this position: move promptly for interim relief once the subsequent sale comes to light (rather than waiting for final hearing), and specifically plead the risk of dissipation of sale proceeds, not just the lis pendens point, to support a deposit direction
This complements, rather than duplicates, general guidance on choosing between specific performance and damages for breach of a sale agreement
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: confirmed: Delhi High Court granted an interim injunction and status quo, and directed a seller to deposit Rs. 20.5 crore in court, after a subsequent sale of a property during a pending specific-performance suit, expressly on a prima facie basis (July 2026, Greater Kailash property)

note: the availability and quantum of any such deposit direction is discretionary and fact-specific (e.g. depends on amounts actually received by the seller on resale) — this should be presented as an available tool, not a guaranteed or formulaic remedy

topic_title: You Paid Off the Company's Loan as Guarantor — Does That Make You a 'Financial Creditor' in Its Insolvency?
angle: A guide for personal guarantors and promoters who have personally settled or paid down a corporate debtor's debt, on why that payment alone does not make them a financial creditor (or let them block/withdraw an ongoing liquidation), and what formal steps actually would.
key_points: A personal guarantor who pays a company's lender out of pocket under a one-time settlement, and gets the lender to close the account, does not thereby automatically acquire that lender's rights as a 'financial creditor' of the company in its own insolvency/liquidation

To actually step into the original lender's shoes, the guarantor needs either (a) a formal assignment of the debt in their favour, or (b) a court/tribunal-ordered substitution as the creditor in the insolvency proceedings — payment and an account-closure certificate from the bank are not a substitute for either

Absent that formal step, a guarantor who has bought the company's assets in connection with the settlement may at most be treated as an asset purchaser/promoter, not as a creditor with standing to seek withdrawal of liquidation or participate in creditor decision-making

An earlier, unchallenged order rejecting a guarantor's attempt to stop liquidation on the same 'I settled the debt' basis will be treated as final and binding, and cannot be relitigated through a fresh application dressed up differently

Practical step for a guarantor planning to settle and then seek a role in the insolvency process: negotiate and document a formal assignment of the debt (or apply for substitution) as part of the settlement itself, rather than relying on an account-closure certificate to establish standing later
This is a narrower, insolvency-specific companion to general guidance on invoking (or resisting) a personal loan guarantee
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: confirmed: NCLAT held a personal guarantor who settled a company's bank debt did not acquire financial creditor status absent an assignment or ordered substitution, and could at most be seen as an asset purchaser (Oct 2026, S.V. Ramasamy re: Swastik Spinners)

topic_title: GST on Corporate Guarantees Between Related Parties: Rule 28(2) and the 1% Deemed Value Explained
angle: A guide for corporate groups on when a parent/holding company's guarantee for a subsidiary attracts GST, how the 1% deemed-value rule actually works after being read down, and how to structure guarantee fees to avoid the default valuation.
key_points: A corporate guarantee given by a holding company for its subsidiary is treated as a taxable supply of service under GST even where no separate fee is charged

Rule 28(2) of the CGST Rules, effective from 26 October 2023, deems the value of such a guarantee at 1% of the amount guaranteed per annum (or the actual consideration, whichever is higher) absent a specific valuation mechanism

Gujarat High Court has read down the words 'whichever is higher' as arbitrary: where actual, ascertainable consideration is charged (even below 1%), GST applies to that actual consideration, and the 1% deemed value applies only where the guarantee is gratuitous or its value cannot otherwise be determined
Rule 28(2) cannot be applied to levy GST for any period before 26 October 2023 — guarantees already in force after that date become taxable from that date onward, not retrospectively

Practical structuring point: a group that charges and can document a genuine, ascertainable guarantee commission (even a modest one) is on stronger ground than one relying on an unstated/gratuitous guarantee that defaults to the 1% figure

This interacts with Section 15(4) of the CGST Act on related-party valuation generally, so guarantee fee-setting should be reviewed alongside the group's broader related-party transfer pricing/valuation documentation
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: confirmed: Gujarat High Court (Torrent Power Ltd. v. Union of India, Aug 2026) upheld Rule 28(2) and Section 15(4) but read down 'whichever is higher', and held the rule is not retrospective to periods before 26 October 2023
note: whether this ruling has been appealed or stayed should be checked before publication, and the position in other High Courts should be noted if they diverge

topic_title: Order XXXVII Summary Suits: How Banks and NBFCs Recover Debt Faster Than an Ordinary Civil Suit
angle: A guide for lenders (and defendants facing one) on when the Order XXXVII summary suit procedure is available, how 'leave to defend' and 'conditional leave to defend' actually work, and what happens if a defendant fails to comply with a conditional leave order.
key_points: Order XXXVII CPC provides a summary procedure for specific classes of suits — principally those founded on a negotiable instrument, or seeking recovery of a debt or liquidated demand in money, including loan/guarantee recovery suits
Its purpose is to prevent a defendant with no genuine triable defence from dragging out litigation through an ordinary, full-length civil suit
A defendant must apply for and be granted 'leave to defend'; the court assesses whether the proposed defence is genuinely triable or merely illusory/moonshine

Courts can grant conditional leave to defend — allowing the defence to proceed only if the defendant deposits the claimed amount (or furnishes equivalent security) in court — particularly where the defence looks triable but weak or vague

Failure to comply with a conditional leave order (e.g. not depositing the required sum within the time given) is treated as fatal: the defendant is barred from contesting the claim further, and the plaintiff becomes entitled to a decree effectively forthwith

Loan documents relied on in such a suit must be properly stamped; courts have allowed a plaintiff to cure an insufficient-stamping defect mid-suit by paying the deficit stamp duty and filing the adjudication order, rather than losing the suit outright on that technicality
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: confirmed: Bombay High Court decreed four IL&FS Order XXXVII summary suits (totalling ~Rs 848.80 crore) after defendants failed to comply with a conditional leave to defend deposit condition (Aug 2026)

note: the exact time limit typically given for compliance with a conditional leave order is case-specific (set by the court in each order), not a fixed statutory period, and should be described as such

topic_title: Can the Government Revise Mining Royalty Rates Mid-Lease? What a Silent Lease Deed Doesn't Protect
angle: A guide for mining lessees on whether a state government can increase royalty/dead rent during the term of an existing lease, and why a lease deed's silence on royalty revision does not freeze the rate for the full lease term.
key_points: A mining lessee does not acquire a vested right to a static, unchanging royalty rate for the life of the lease merely because the lease deed itself contains no express royalty-revision clause

The power to revise royalty and dead rent during a subsisting lease derives from the governing mining statute and rules (and any state notification issued under them), not from an express term in the lease deed — so its absence from the deed is not a bar

The Supreme Court has set aside a High Court order that had blocked a state's royalty/dead-rate enhancement on exactly this reasoning, confirming the government's statutory power to revise survives a silent lease deed
Lessees should budget for periodic royalty revisions as a matter of regulatory risk, rather than treating the rate fixed at the time of grant as fixed for the lease's duration

This sits alongside, and should be read together with, the separate question of how stamp duty on a mining lease itself is computed (generally on anticipated royalty yield, not dead rent) — the two are related but distinct cost considerations for a prospective lessee
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: confirmed: Supreme Court (State of Haryana v. Faridabad Gurgaon Minerals, 2026 INSC 690, July 2026) held a lessee cannot claim a vested right to static royalty merely because the lease deed is silent on revision, and upheld the state's statutory power to revise mid-lease

topic_title: Stamp Duty on Mining Leases: Why It's Calculated on Anticipated Royalty, Not Dead Rent
angle: A guide for a company negotiating or executing a mining lease on how the upfront stamp duty is actually computed in states that value the lease by reference to anticipated royalty yield rather than the (lower) dead rent figure, and why this materially affects upfront transaction cost.
key_points: Mining leases typically fix both a 'dead rent' (a minimum fixed payment regardless of extraction) and a royalty (payable per unit of mineral actually extracted, usually far exceeding dead rent once production ramps up)

Several states have notified that stamp duty on a mining lease instrument should be computed by reference to the anticipated royalty yield over the lease term, rather than the much lower dead rent figure — which the Supreme Court has upheld as not ultra vires Section 26 of the Indian Stamp Act, 1899

This means the stamp duty payable on executing a mining lease can be substantially higher than a dead-rent-based calculation would suggest, and should be factored into deal cost projections before execution, not discovered only at registration

The validity of a particular state's anticipated-royalty stamp duty notification should be checked against that state's specific notification, since not every state necessarily uses the same valuation basis
This question is distinct from, though related to, the separate question of whether and when the government can revise the royalty rate itself during the lease term
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: confirmed: Supreme Court (Birla Corporation Ltd. v. State of Madhya Pradesh, July 2026) upheld Madhya Pradesh's 1993 notification computing mining-lease stamp duty on anticipated royalty rather than dead rent, as not ultra vires Section 26 of the Indian Stamp Act

note: this guide should flag that the anticipated-royalty basis is confirmed for Madhya Pradesh's specific notification — readers in other states should check their own state's stamp valuation rules for mining leases rather than assume the same basis applies uniformly

topic_title: IBC vs RERA: Which Law Actually Wins When a Homebuyer's Rights Conflict With an Approved Resolution Plan
angle: A guide for homebuyers in a real estate company's CIRP on why an approved resolution plan can override individual RERA refund/possession rights, how the homebuyer class votes through its Authorised Representative, and what a dissenting minority buyer can (and cannot) still do.
key_points: Once a real estate corporate debtor enters CIRP, homebuyers participate in the Committee of Creditors as a class through a single Authorised Representative, who votes the class's collective voting share based on instructions from, or the majority view of, represented homebuyers

Where the class (through its Authorised Representative) approves a resolution plan, individual dissenting homebuyers holding only a small fraction of the class's voting share cannot unilaterally demand a separate exit/refund mechanism for themselves outside the approved plan

Section 238 of the IBC gives the Code overriding effect over other laws to the extent of any inconsistency — tribunals have relied on this to hold the Code's class-based resolution mechanism prevails over an individual buyer's RERA-based refund expectation once a plan is approved

A buyer who disagrees with the approved plan's treatment of homebuyers generally has the route of challenging the plan's approval itself (on the ground it is not compliant with the Code, e.g. unfair/discriminatory treatment within the homebuyer class) rather than seeking a standalone refund order outside the plan

Practical takeaway for buyers: engage actively with the Authorised Representative and the plan approval process itself (objections, voting instructions) rather than waiting to raise refund objections only after the plan is approved, since post-approval individual relief is very difficult to obtain

This is distinct from the separate question of whether pending RERA proceedings bar admission of an insolvency petition in the first place — that is a threshold question, answered differently from what a buyer can get once CIRP is already underway and a plan is approved
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: confirmed: NCLT Mumbai dismissed four dissenting homebuyers' (0.22% voting share) bid for an individual refund mechanism after the homebuyer class (22.66% voting share, via its Authorised Representative) had approved the Spenta Enclave resolution plan, holding the Code's provisions prevail over inconsistent individual refund rights (Sept 2026)

topic_title: Suing Over Defective Seeds: What a Farmer Must Prove (and What a Seed Company Can Use as a Defence)
angle: A guide for farmers pursuing a consumer complaint over crop failure from allegedly defective seed, and for seed companies defending such claims, on how courts actually weigh a field inspection report and apportion liability between seed defect and natural/weather factors.
key_points: The Seeds Act, 1966 regulates only notified varieties and provides no direct compensation remedy for a farmer suffering loss from poor seed quality — which is why farmers typically pursue relief through consumer fora under the Consumer Protection Act instead

A district consumer forum/commission will often rely on an independent field inspection report assessing the actual extent of crop development/failure, rather than accepting the farmer's account of total crop loss at face value

Where an inspection report attributes the shortfall to a mix of causes — partial seed-related failure alongside genuine natural factors such as excessive rainfall — courts have declined to find 'complete deficiency of service' by the seller, and apportioned compensation rather than awarding full claimed loss

Practical evidentiary point for farmers: a prompt, properly documented field inspection (ideally jointly conducted or at least with notice to the seller) strengthens a claim far more than post-hoc assertions about total yield failure

Practical point for seed companies: weather/rainfall data and inspection findings showing partial pod/crop development, rather than complete failure, are central to limiting liability to a genuine proportion of loss
This guide complements, and should be read alongside, general consumer-complaint procedure guidance, since the forum and filing process itself follows the ordinary Consumer Protection Act route
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: confirmed: Supreme Court (M/s Shyam Beej Bhandar v. Suresh, 2026 INSC 158, Feb 2026) apportioned compensation rather than awarding full relief, based on a field inspection report showing natural factors (excessive rainfall) significantly contributed to groundnut crop shortfall alongside any seed-quality issue

topic_title: Can a Privatised PSU Still Be Sued by Writ Petition? What Air India's Post-Disinvestment Cases Show
angle: A guide for employees and other claimants with a pre-disinvestment dispute against a since-privatised public sector company, on when Article 226 writ jurisdiction remains available despite the company no longer being 'State' for constitutional purposes.
key_points: Once a public sector company is fully disinvested/privatised, it generally ceases to be 'State' under Article 12, and ordinary post-privatisation employment or contractual claims against it as a private employer are not amenable to writ jurisdiction

Courts have drawn a distinction, however, for challenges that target not the privatised company as an employer but a pre-existing tribunal's award or adjudicatory process from a dispute that arose and was being adjudicated before the disinvestment took effect

Where the writ petition's real target is the earlier Industrial Tribunal's award/process (e.g. an inadequate compensation award for a pre-privatisation termination), courts have held the company's current private ownership does not bar the writ, since the petition is not against the company as a private employer but against the award and the statutory adjudicatory process itself

Practical implication: a claimant with a stale industrial dispute predating a PSU's privatisation should not assume writ jurisdiction is automatically closed off — the framing of the challenge (tribunal award/process vs. the company's current private conduct) is decisive
This narrow route does not reopen the broader, settled position that a privatised company's day-to-day employment decisions after disinvestment are not themselves subject to writ review

Relevant higher authority on the broader question (whether a privatised PSU remains amenable to writ jurisdiction at all) should be checked, since the Supreme Court has separately examined this issue and any later ruling should be read alongside the Air India line of cases
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: confirmed: Delhi High Court (Sauraj Singh v. M/s Indian Airlines Ltd., 2026 DHC 4055, May 2026) held a writ challenging a pre-privatisation CGIT award remains maintainable against the now-privatised Air India, distinguishing ordinary post-privatisation employment claims

note: this is a narrow, fact-specific line of authority (tribunal-award challenges predating disinvestment) and should not be presented as a general rule that privatised PSUs remain amenable to writ jurisdiction for all purposes

topic_title: NHAI Toll Operator Revenue-Loss Claims: Proving Losses From Incorrect Toll Rates and COD Delays
angle: A guide for highway toll concessionaires on how to build and prove a revenue-loss claim against NHAI arising from incorrectly fixed toll rates, delayed declaration of the Commercial Operation Date (COD), or mandated free-pass obligations to local residents.
key_points: Common categories of toll-operator revenue-loss claims against NHAI include: toll rates fixed at an incorrect (too low) level relative to the concession terms, delay in NHAI declaring the Commercial Operation Date (which affects when toll collection and revenue entitlement actually begins), and the cost burden of mandated free monthly passes for local residents near a toll plaza

Arbitral tribunals assessing such claims look for concrete, quantified evidence of the loss attributable to each specific cause — a bundled, undifferentiated loss figure is harder to sustain than separately evidenced heads of claim

Courts reviewing a resulting award under Section 34 give the tribunal's factual findings on these questions considerable deference, intervening only where the tribunal's interpretation is not even a plausible reading of the concession agreement — so a well-evidenced award in the concessionaire's favour is difficult for NHAI to overturn on appeal

Practical evidentiary steps for a concessionaire: maintain contemporaneous toll-collection data broken down by period and cause, document the actual COD declaration timeline against the concession schedule, and separately track the cost of any mandated free-pass obligations

This is distinct from force-majeure-based concession-extension claims (e.g. for COVID-19 disruption), which involve a different analytical question — extension of the concession term itself, rather than a revenue-loss damages claim for a specific period
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: confirmed: Delhi High Court upheld an arbitral award of about Rs 12.18 crore to a Kerala toll concessionaire (Kochi Aroor Tollways) against NHAI for losses tied to incorrectly fixed toll rates, delayed COD declaration, and free local-resident pass costs (Jan 2026)

topic_title: Letter of Comfort vs Bank Guarantee: Why the Difference Decides Whether a Parent Company Actually Pays
angle: A guide for lenders and corporate groups on the legal distinction between a letter of comfort and a formal guarantee, when a letter of comfort is nonetheless enforceable, and the drafting choices that determine which a given document actually is.
key_points: A formal guarantee must satisfy the requirements of Section 126 of the Indian Contract Act and typically creates a clear, direct payment obligation enforceable against the guarantor on the principal debtor's default

A letter of comfort is typically a softer assurance — often issued by a parent company for a subsidiary's borrowing — that does not necessarily satisfy formal guarantee requirements, but courts have nonetheless treated a sufficiently specific letter of comfort as an enforceable promise in its own right, separate from the Contract Act's guarantee formalities

Courts have invoked the 'group of companies' doctrine to bind a parent company to an arbitration clause in a loan agreement based on its letter of comfort, where the parent was sufficiently involved in the underlying transaction's negotiation and performance

On the other hand, tribunals have also held that an entity issuing a mere letter of comfort is not thereby a 'corporate debtor' or 'guarantor' for IBC purposes, where the letter does not create an actual financial/operational debt obligation — so the enforceability of a letter of comfort is highly fact- and wording-dependent, not automatic either way

Practical drafting point for a lender: if a genuine, directly enforceable payment obligation from the parent is wanted, a formal Section 126-compliant guarantee is far more reliable than a letter of comfort, however strongly worded; a letter of comfort leaves real enforceability risk and litigation uncertainty

Practical point for a parent company: a letter of comfort is not 'risk-free' comfort-only language — depending on its specificity and the surrounding conduct, it can still be read as an enforceable promise or used to bind the parent to an arbitration clause
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: confirmed: Delhi High Court has held a letter of comfort can be enforceable as a promise even without satisfying Section 126 guarantee formalities, and has referred claims under letters of comfort to arbitration via the group-of-companies doctrine (Essel Group matter)
confirmed: NCLT Delhi has separately held an entity issuing a letter of comfort is not a corporate debtor or guarantor under the IBC where no actual operational debt arises from it
note: these two lines of authority address different questions (civil/contractual enforceability vs IBC debt characterisation) and should be presented as complementary, not conflicting

topic_title: Medical Negligence Claims: Why a Hospital's Failure to Produce the Complete Case Sheet Can Decide the Case
angle: A guide for patients/families pursuing a medical negligence complaint, and for hospitals defending one, on the evidentiary significance of the hospital's medical records and case sheet, and what an incomplete or withheld record actually does to the burden of proof.
key_points: A complete, contemporaneously maintained case sheet and treatment record is the primary documentary evidence of what was actually done for a patient and why — its completeness (or lack of it) is heavily scrutinised by consumer commissions assessing a negligence complaint

Where a hospital cannot produce a complete case sheet, or cannot adequately justify a specific clinical decision (such as administering a particular treatment to a patient with a known contraindicating condition) from the records it does produce, commissions have treated this gap itself as supporting a negligence finding, not merely as a procedural shortcoming

This differs from, but interacts with, the general principle that the complainant bears the initial burden of establishing a deficiency in service — a hospital's inability to produce adequate records can shift the practical weight of that burden once a prima facie concern is raised

Practical point for hospitals/healthcare providers: maintaining and being able to promptly produce complete, contemporaneous records is not just good clinical practice but a central legal defence — gaps discovered only during litigation are difficult to explain away after the fact

Practical point for complainants: a formal request for the complete treatment record/case sheet early in the dispute (before filing, if possible) both supports the claim's evidentiary basis and tests whether the hospital can actually produce what it should have maintained

This guide is distinct from the general 'medical negligence: consumer, civil and criminal routes' overview already on the site — it focuses specifically on the evidentiary weight of record-keeping failures within whichever route is chosen
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: confirmed: Kakinada District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission held a hospital and treating cardiologist liable for Rs 99 lakh partly because they failed to produce the complete case sheet and treatment records and could not justify administering dialysis to a cardiac patient (Aug 2026)

topic_title: When Can a GST Writ Petition Be Dismissed for 'Misleading the Court'? Lessons From Repeat Litigation Over Fake ITC
angle: A guide for taxpayers (and their counsel) facing a fake/fraudulent ITC demand under Section 74, on why a writ petition is usually the wrong route when a statutory appeal exists, and the specific litigation-conduct risk of denying or misdescribing an earlier related proceeding to the court.
key_points: Where a statutory appellate remedy under Section 107 of the CGST Act is available and adequate, High Courts have consistently held a writ petition challenging a fake/fraudulent ITC demand is not maintainable merely because the taxpayer would prefer to bypass the appeal route

Courts treat this especially strictly in fake-ITC matters, given the fact-intensive nature of such disputes, which are generally better suited to the appellate authority's fuller fact-finding process than to writ jurisdiction's limited scope of review

A litigation-conduct risk distinct from the merits: where counsel denies or misdescribes to the court that an earlier, connected proceeding (e.g. by a sister concern operating from the same premises, challenging the same show cause notice) exists or was withdrawn, and the record contradicts that denial, courts have treated this as the court being misled — an independent, aggravating ground for dismissal

Practical point for taxpayers with related/group entities facing parallel or connected GST proceedings: disclose the full procedural history of all connected matters to counsel and ensure it is accurately placed before the court, since omissions here can taint an otherwise arguable case

Practical point generally: before filing a writ in a fake-ITC matter, assess honestly whether the statutory appeal route is genuinely inadequate (e.g. true breach of natural justice) rather than simply less convenient, since 'alternative remedy exists' is likely to be the court's first and dispositive response
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: confirmed: Gujarat High Court (Mahalaxmi Industries v. Union of India, July 2026) dismissed a writ challenging a ~Rs 1.47 crore fake-ITC demand both for the existence of an adequate statutory appeal and because counsel had misled the court about a sister concern's earlier, connected writ petition

topic_title: SEBI's Settlement Mechanism: How Proceedings Get Settled Without Admission of Guilt
angle: A guide for companies and individuals facing SEBI enforcement action on how the settlement route under the SEBI (Settlement Proceedings) Regulations actually works, what 'without admitting or denying' really means in practice, and the risk that a settled matter can still be revived.
key_points: SEBI's settlement framework lets a person against whom proceedings have been initiated (or are reasonably apprehended) apply to settle by paying a settlement amount and/or undertaking specific actions, without admitting or denying the underlying findings of fact or conclusions of law

Settlement applications are considered by a panel (typically including Whole-Time Members) which evaluates and approves settlement terms; approval is not automatic and SEBI retains discretion over whether a matter is appropriate for settlement at all

'Without admitting or denying' matters practically: a settlement order is generally not treated as a factual finding of wrongdoing, which can be relevant to collateral proceedings, but it does not erase the underlying conduct or prevent SEBI's own records of the investigation from existing

SEBI has expressly retained the power to revive settled proceedings where there is a false representation, breach of the settlement undertaking, or any discrepancy in the settlement terms as actually implemented — settlement is not an unconditional, permanently final closure

High-value, high-profile respondents have used the settlement route for matters spanning years-long investigations (e.g. minimum public shareholding non-compliance), confirming it is not limited to minor or technical violations

SEBI issued a 2026 consultation paper proposing a full overhaul of the settlement mechanism through new Settlement of Proceedings Regulations, so the current framework may change — practitioners should check the regulations actually in force at the time of any application
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: confirmed: four Adani group companies and several individuals settled SEBI MPS proceedings in September 2026 under the current settlement framework, without admission or denial, with SEBI retaining revival power
confirmed: SEBI issued an August 2026 consultation paper proposing a full overhaul of the settlement regulations

note: the exact current regulations in force (SEBI (Settlement Proceedings) Regulations, 2018, as amended) versus any newly notified 2026 regulations should be checked at time of publication, since the consultation paper may have since been finalised

topic_title: Minimum Public Shareholding Non-Compliance: What Listed Companies and Promoters Actually Risk
angle: A guide for listed companies and their promoters on the consequences of falling short of the minimum public shareholding (MPS) requirement, from SEBI's enforcement escalation path to the recent example of a major group settling MPS proceedings years after the underlying non-compliance.
key_points: Listed companies must maintain a minimum public shareholding (generally 25%, with specific carve-outs/timelines for certain categories) under SEBI's Securities Contracts (Regulation) Rules framework

Enforcement typically escalates through the stock exchanges first: on finding non-compliance, an exchange issues a notice (generally within a set number of days of discovery) and advises the entity to achieve compliance within a prescribed period

Consequences for continued non-compliance can include freezing of promoter shareholding/voting rights and corporate benefits in proportion to the extent of non-compliance, restrictions on promoters/directors taking new board positions at other listed companies, and monetary penalties (potentially substantial under the governing securities law)

MPS investigations can run for years before resolution — the recent Adani group MPS settlement traced back to a 2020 complaint, with show cause notices issued only in 2024-25 and settlement finally concluded in 2026, illustrating how long such matters can remain open

Settlement under SEBI's settlement framework is available even for MPS non-compliance, letting a company and its directors close out the matter by payment without admitting the underlying findings — but this does not retroactively cure the period of actual non-compliance for other purposes

Practical takeaway for companies approaching an MPS threshold risk (e.g. after a promoter share pledge enforcement, or corporate restructuring that concentrates promoter holding): proactively plan a compliance pathway (OFS, QIP, rights issue, etc.) well before any exchange notice, since the enforcement consequences escalate the longer non-compliance continues
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: confirmed: four Adani group companies and associated individuals settled MPS non-compliance proceedings with SEBI for Rs 37.05 lakh each (plus separate individual settlements) in September 2026, a matter traced back to a 2020 complaint

note: the current MPS percentage threshold and specific exchange-notice timelines should be re-confirmed against the current SCRR and SEBI circulars in force at time of writing, since this framework has been revised over time (the description above reflects the general, settled 2013/2017-era framework)

topic_title: Is a Development Authority a RERA 'Promoter'? The Pre-Act Land Acquisition Question
angle: A guide for allottees of residential layouts developed by a statutory development authority (e.g. a Bangalore-, Delhi- or state-level development authority) on the live legal question of whether such an authority counts as a RERA 'promoter' for layouts where the underlying land acquisition predates the RERA Act, and what this means for a buyer's remedies in the meantime.
key_points: RERA defines 'promoter' broadly under Section 2(zk), and state RERA authorities/appellate tribunals have in several instances held that a statutory development authority developing and allotting residential layouts falls within that definition, exposing it to RERA's registration and disclosure obligations and to buyer complaints

A development authority has argued, with at least interim success in one state, that RERA should not apply to layouts where the preliminary land-acquisition notification predates the RERA Act's commencement — reasoning that the project's foundational legal basis arose under an entirely different, pre-existing statutory scheme

This question remains genuinely unsettled as of 2026 — at least one High Court has granted only an interim stay of RERA's applicability to a specific authority's pre-Act layouts, without deciding the underlying question, so the position can differ by state and project

Practical implication for an allottee in a development-authority layout: check whether the specific project's land acquisition predates RERA and whether any court proceeding is live on this point in that state before assuming a RERA complaint is the right forum — a parallel civil or statutory remedy specific to that development authority's own enabling Act may need to be pursued instead or in addition

Buyers should not simply wait for the broader legal question to be resolved if their claim has its own limitation concerns — filing in the forum currently available (even if its jurisdiction is contested) preserves the buyer's position better than waiting
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: confirmed: Karnataka High Court granted the Bangalore Development Authority an interim stay of RERA's applicability to specific layouts predating the Act's commencement, with the broader question still undecided (June 2026)

note: this is a single state's interim order on a specific authority — the guide should make clear this is not a settled, generally applicable rule, and other states' authorities and courts may take a different view

topic_title: Avoiding a Preferential or Fraudulent Transaction in Liquidation: Why Proper Notice to Erstwhile Management Actually Matters
angle: A guide for liquidators and resolution professionals on the procedural (not just substantive) requirements for a successful Section 43/66 avoidance application, focusing specifically on serving proper notice on the corporate debtor's suspended/erstwhile management.
key_points: A transaction audit report flagging transactions as preferential (Section 43) or fraudulent/for extortionate credit (Sections 66/50) is an important evidentiary foundation for an avoidance application, but it is not by itself sufficient to secure an order

Tribunals have dismissed otherwise well-evidenced avoidance applications where the liquidator failed to ensure proper statutory notice of the application was actually served on the corporate debtor's suspended board/erstwhile management — a pure procedural defect, separate from the substantive merits of the avoidance claim

This means a liquidator's procedural checklist (confirming service, keeping proof of service, following up on defective service) is as important to the ultimate success of an avoidance application as the quality of the underlying transaction audit itself

A liquidator whose avoidance application is dismissed purely for a notice defect generally retains the ability to refile properly once service is correctly effected, provided limitation has not separately run out — so the setback, while costly in time, is not necessarily fatal to recovering the transaction's value

This complements, rather than duplicates, general guidance on the categories of avoidable transactions under the IBC — it focuses specifically on the procedural service requirement that liquidators sometimes overlook
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: confirmed: NCLT Ahmedabad dismissed a liquidator's ~Rs 2.50 crore preferential/fraudulent transaction avoidance application for failure to properly serve statutory notice on the suspended management, despite a transaction audit report supporting the claim (2026 TAXSCAN (NCLT) 202)

topic_title: Removed the Dark Pattern After Getting Caught? Why That Doesn't Erase CCPA Liability
angle: A guide for e-commerce, ed-tech and other digital platforms on why voluntarily removing a dark pattern after receiving a CCPA notice does not absolve liability for the period the practice was actually live, with practical guidance on proactive self-audits versus reactive fixes.
key_points: The CCPA's dark pattern guidelines identify several prohibited categories, including 'basket sneaking' — adding an item, donation or charge to a transaction (often via a pre-ticked checkbox) that the consumer must affirmatively notice and deselect rather than affirmatively opt into

The CCPA has expressly held that a platform's post-notice removal of a dark pattern (even where done promptly and in apparent good faith as a compliance step) does not absolve liability for violations already committed during the period the practice was live

Aggregate exposure from a dark pattern can be assessed by reference to how much revenue/benefit it generated and how many users were affected, not merely the per-transaction amount — a small per-transaction figure (e.g. a modest default donation) can still produce a large aggregate finding once multiplied across millions of users over an extended period

Practical implication: platforms should treat CCPA's self-audit directions (which have been issued broadly across the e-commerce sector) as a genuine proactive compliance exercise, not a box-ticking response only after a specific complaint or notice — by the time a notice arrives, the liability window for past conduct has typically already closed in the regulator's favour

A compliance report deadline (commonly around 15 days from an order) is typically imposed alongside any penalty, so platforms found in violation should have an implementation plan ready to action immediately, not merely a plan to eventually comply
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: confirmed: CCPA penalised PhysicsWallah Rs 5 lakh for a pre-ticked donation dark pattern (classed as basket sneaking) and held that removing the feature after notice did not absolve liability for the period it was active (order dated 1 June 2026)
note: this guide should avoid suggesting the Rs 5 lakh figure is any kind of cap or benchmark — CCPA penalty amounts vary by case and this guide should present it only as an illustrative example

topic_title: You Proved Your Retrenchment Was Illegal — So Why Didn't the Court Give You Your Job Back?
angle: A guide for workmen (and employers) on why establishing an illegal retrenchment under Section 25F of the Industrial Disputes Act does not automatically entitle a worker to reinstatement or regularisation, and what courts actually weigh in deciding between reinstatement, regularisation and compensation.
key_points: Proving a retrenchment violated the mandatory conditions of Section 25F (notice/wages in lieu, and retrenchment compensation) establishes that the termination was illegal, but that finding alone does not dictate the remedy — reinstatement, regularisation into a permanent post, and monetary compensation are distinct forms of relief, each with its own threshold

Courts/tribunals have held that ordering regularisation into permanent employment exceeds a Labour Court's jurisdiction where regularisation was never specifically claimed as relief in the industrial dispute, and where the worker's actual period of engagement before termination was brief

Long delay in the litigation itself (industrial disputes spanning decades are not unusual) is a factor courts weigh against ordering reinstatement, since reinstating someone into a role and workplace that has moved on after 20-30 years is often treated as impractical — compensation is substituted instead, sometimes substantially increased to reflect the delay and the inadequacy of an originally meagre award

Practical point for a workman: if regularisation or a permanent post is genuinely sought as the remedy (not just reinstatement to the same type of role), it should be specifically pleaded as relief in the industrial dispute itself, rather than assumed to follow automatically from an illegality finding

Practical point for employers: an illegal retrenchment finding is not an automatic path to a large reinstatement-driven liability — courts will look closely at what relief was actually sought, how long the worker was engaged, and how long the matter has been pending in deciding the appropriate remedy
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: confirmed: Delhi High Court (SBI v. Umed Singh, 2026 LiveLaw (Del) 639) upheld an illegal-retrenchment finding but set aside a regularisation order, substituting Rs 1 lakh compensation, noting the brief original engagement and that regularisation was never specifically sought as relief (July 2026)

confirmed: Delhi High Court (Sauraj Singh v. Air India, 2026 DHC 4055) tripled a 1998 CGIT compensation award after declining reinstatement given a 25-year delay (May 2026) — illustrating the same reinstatement-vs-compensation tradeoff from the opposite direction (worker got more compensation, not reinstatement)

topic_title: Can a Country Claim Exclusive Rights Over a Product's Generic Name? What the Pisco GI Dispute Decided
angle: A guide to the limits of Geographical Indication protection, explaining why claiming a composite, qualified GI (e.g. 'Peruvian Pisco') does not extend to monopolising the underlying generic product name itself, and what this means for producers and importers of similarly-named products from multiple origin countries.
key_points: Geographical Indication protection in India is not automatic for any term with a geographic connotation — it must be specifically claimed through a properly scoped GI application, and is subject to the GI Act's absolute grounds of refusal

Where a product name (such as 'Pisco') is used by producers from more than one country and has itself become understood as a generic product category rather than an indicator tied exclusively to one geographic origin, a court can decline to grant one country's producers exclusive rights over the bare, standalone term

A country/producer group can still obtain and enforce protection for a composite, qualified GI (e.g. 'Peruvian Pisco' specifically) even where the bare underlying term itself cannot be monopolised — the qualified, composite form remains distinct from, and narrower than, exclusive control of the generic term

This has practical consequences for importers/distributors and other origin countries' producers: they generally remain free to use the generic product term itself (subject to not misleadingly suggesting an exclusive-origin claim they don't have), even where one country holds a composite GI

This nuance is distinct from, and should not be confused with, India's general GI registration and enforcement framework (covered elsewhere) — it specifically addresses what happens when a GI claim runs up against a term's generic/non-exclusive character
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: confirmed: Delhi High Court Division Bench dismissed the Embassy of Peru's appeal seeking exclusive GI rights over the standalone term 'Pisco', while confirming Peru's protection extends to the composite GI 'Peruvian Pisco' (March 2026)

topic_title: FSSAI's Batch-Specific Recall Findings: Why One Unsafe Batch Doesn't Condemn Your Whole Product Line
angle: A guide for food manufacturers and distributors on the legal and reputational scope of an FSSAI recall order tied to a specific batch, how to communicate the batch-specific nature of a finding to trade partners and consumers, and what it does not establish about the rest of the product line.
key_points: An FSSAI recall order triggered by an unsafe sample is legally and procedurally tied to the specific batch(es) tested, identified by batch/lot number, not the product line as a whole

FSSAI itself has, in recent recall orders, expressly clarified that a batch-specific unsafe finding should not be read as condemning all of a manufacturer's products under that name -- a point manufacturers should proactively repeat in their own consumer communications rather than leaving the ambiguity to spread on its own

The Food Recall Procedure Regulations, 2017 require the food business operator to identify the affected batch(es), execute the recall plan, and submit recall status reports and records of recovered product, but this process-compliance obligation is distinct from, and narrower than, a product-wide safety claim

A manufacturer facing a batch-specific recall should preserve and be ready to produce batch-tracking and quality-control records for both the affected and unaffected batches, since the ability to show clear traceability is what actually substantiates the batch-specific, not product-wide, distinction if challenged

Overreacting publicly (e.g. a blanket, product-line-wide statement) can do more commercial damage than the regulatory finding itself -- communications should mirror the actual legal scope of the recall

This is a narrower companion to the site's general FSSAI Food Recall Procedure guide, focused specifically on managing the scope and framing of a recall once issued, rather than the compliance mechanics of executing one
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: confirmed: FSSAI expressly stated, in ordering a recall of a specific Everest cumin powder batch for pesticide residues, that the finding related only to the implicated batch and should not be read as applying to all Everest cumin powder products (Oct 2026)
