note: this guide should rely on the general Food Recall Procedure Regulations, 2017 framework for the compliance mechanics, cross-referencing the site's existing recall-procedure guide rather than restating it

topic_title: Appointing a Court Commissioner to Inspect or Secure Disputed Assets: What Order XXVI CPC Actually Allows
angle: A practical guide for a litigant (in a commercial, property, or arbitration-interim-relief dispute) on when a court will appoint a Local Commissioner to inspect, inventory or take custody of disputed property/assets pending final adjudication, and how this differs from a final finding on entitlement.
key_points: Order XXVI of the CPC empowers a court to appoint a commissioner for specific purposes including making a local investigation, inspecting property, or preparing an inventory of movable property -- a practical tool for preserving evidence and the parties' relative positions while a dispute is pending

Courts have used this power in support of interim relief in commercial and arbitration-related proceedings (e.g. under Section 9 of the Arbitration Act) -- appointing a Local Commissioner to inspect and inventory a party's assets at a disputed property while the underlying dispute is referred to arbitration or trial

Appointing a Local Commissioner for inspection/inventory is squarely an interim, preservation-oriented step -- it does not itself decide who is entitled to the assets or property, and courts are careful to frame such orders as not prejudging the merits

A party seeking this relief should be specific about what the Commissioner is being asked to do (inspect, inventory, take custody, or some combination), since the scope of the Commissioner's mandate is defined by the court's order, not assumed from the general power

This tool is frequently paired with other interim relief (such as a status quo injunction or a direction to deposit disputed funds in court) rather than used alone, since inventorying assets does not by itself prevent their removal or dissipation absent an accompanying restraint

Practical tip: a party opposing such an application should focus on narrowing its scope (e.g. objecting to custody being taken, while not objecting to a mere inspection/inventory) rather than resisting the appointment outright, since courts are generally receptive to at least the inspection/inventory form of this relief
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: confirmed: Delhi High Court appointed a Local Commissioner to inspect and inventory a party's assets at a disputed leased property, alongside referring the underlying lease dispute to arbitration, in a Section 9 interim-relief application (Amazon Seller Services v. Goodluck Buildtech, Sept 2026)

topic_title: Your Personal Guarantee Says 'Capped at Rs X Crore' — Why You Could Still Owe More
angle: A guide for personal guarantors on why a stated principal-liability cap in a Deed of Guarantee often doesn't cap total exposure, because accruing interest from the date of demand is commonly treated as separate from, and additive to, the capped principal.
key_points: A Deed of Guarantee's cap is frequently drafted to apply only to the principal amount guaranteed, with a separate clause fixing an interest rate running from the date of demand — tribunals have held the two operate independently, so accrued interest is added on top of, not absorbed within, the capped figure
This means the guarantor's real-world exposure can exceed the headline cap by a significant margin once interest has run for months or years before the guarantee is actually invoked

Before signing, a guarantor should specifically check whether the cap is drafted as an all-inclusive ceiling (principal + interest + costs) or as a principal-only cap with interest running separately — the two are very different commitments even though both might be marketed as 'a Rs X crore guarantee'

Where the guarantee is already signed and interest has been accruing, a guarantor negotiating settlement should calculate their exposure using the actual interest clause, not just the headline cap figure, to avoid underestimating the settlement needed to close the matter
This is a narrower, guarantee-specific companion to general guidance on invoking (or resisting) a personal loan guarantee already on the site
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: confirmed: NCLAT upheld insolvency proceedings against a personal guarantor whose Deed of Guarantee capped principal liability at Rs 40 crore, holding separately-stipulated interest at 12.70% per annum from the date of demand meant total exposure could exceed the cap (Aug 2026, Nyka Steel/UCO Bank matter)

topic_title: The 30-Day Clock in Liquidation: Why a Secured Creditor Must Elect Fast Under Regulation 21A
angle: A guide for secured creditors (including government departments holding customs/excise bonds or bank guarantees as security) on the mandatory 30-day window to elect whether to relinquish or realise security once a corporate debtor enters liquidation, and the consequence of missing it.
key_points: Regulation 21A of the IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016 requires a secured creditor to inform the liquidator of its decision — relinquish the security to the liquidation estate, or realise it independently — within 30 days of the liquidation commencement date

Tribunals have held that silence within that 30-day window is not neutral: it is treated as a presumed relinquishment, pulling the secured asset (including bank guarantees, FDRs, or bonds held as security) into the liquidation estate for distribution under the Section 53 waterfall

This has been applied even against government departments (e.g. Customs holding bank guarantees/FDRs as security for duty obligations) — sovereign or regulatory status does not exempt a creditor from the same 30-day election requirement

A creditor's later attempt to argue the security should stay earmarked or alive (e.g. because underlying obligations remain unfulfilled) does not override a missed election — the window is treated as a hard procedural deadline, not a negotiable one

Practical point for any secured creditor: liquidation commencement triggers an immediate internal process to identify all security interests held against a corporate debtor and make (and document) the Regulation 21A election well within the 30-day window, rather than treating it as routine paperwork that can wait
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: confirmed: NCLAT upheld release of bank guarantee FDRs worth Rs 89.16 lakh to a liquidation estate because Customs failed to exercise the non-relinquishment option within 30 days under Regulation 21A, despite Customs' claim the guarantees should remain earmarked for unfulfilled export-obligation duty (2026, Metalite Eco Future Labs matter, Company Appeal (AT)(Insolvency) No. 745 of 2025)

topic_title: GST Registration Cancelled Without Reading Your Reply? Here's Your Strongest Ground to Get It Set Aside
angle: A practical guide for a GST-registered business whose registration was cancelled after it filed a substantive reply to the show cause notice, on building and arguing the 'non-application of mind' / natural justice challenge, distinct from challenging the cancellation on its substantive merits.
key_points: Where a taxpayer files a detailed, substantive reply to a GST registration cancellation show cause notice, and the resulting cancellation order shows no engagement with that reply's specific points, High Courts have repeatedly quashed the cancellation for 'non-application of mind' — a distinct, procedural ground from arguing the cancellation is wrong on the facts

Courts look for concrete signs the reply was actually read and considered: specific reasons addressing the taxpayer's points, not just a templated recitation that a reply was 'received and considered' without engagement

This ground has succeeded even where the underlying substantive case for cancellation might otherwise be reasonably arguable — the order can still fall purely for failing to show engagement with the reply, independent of whether the department could ultimately justify cancellation on the merits

Practical step for a taxpayer: when filing a reply to a cancellation SCN, structure it with clearly numbered points addressing each allegation, since a cancellation order's failure to address those same numbered points individually makes the 'non-application of mind' argument far easier to establish on judicial review

Relief typically granted is a quashing with remand for a fresh, reasoned decision after genuine consideration of the reply — not an automatic final win on the merits, so the taxpayer should still be prepared to substantively defend the registration at the fresh hearing
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: confirmed: Punjab & Haryana High Court quashed a GST registration cancellation for non-application of mind where the department ignored the taxpayer's reply to a 12 February 2026 show cause notice (2026)

note: this is one of several similar High Court rulings on the same procedural point (Delhi HC, Allahabad HC and others have reached similar results) — the guide should present this as a now-well-established line of authority, not an isolated ruling

topic_title: Why an 'Accessory' to Your Imported Machine Might Get a Worse Customs Tariff Than the Machine Itself
angle: A guide for importers of peripherals, accessories and add-on devices marketed alongside a parent machine (especially diagnostic/medical/industrial equipment), on why customs authorities and courts often push such accessories into a residuary tariff heading rather than letting them ride on the parent machine's classification.
key_points: An accessory or peripheral device is not automatically entitled to the same favourable tariff classification as the parent machine it is sold or marketed alongside — classification turns on the accessory's own independent function, not its marketing bundle

Where an accessory lacks any independent diagnostic, measuring or other specialised function of its own (for example, a printer or imager that only outputs what another device has already processed), courts have held it cannot be classified under a heading reserved for devices with that independent function, even if the parent machine qualifies for that heading

Such accessories, compatible with machines that might themselves fall under several different tariff headings, have been pushed into the residuary customs tariff heading (e.g. CTH 9033 for apparatus and appliances not elsewhere specified in Chapter 90) — which can carry a different (often higher) duty rate than the parent machine's own heading

Practical step before importing: assess the accessory's actual, independent function separately from the parent machine's marketing description, and model the duty impact under both the preferred and the residuary classification before committing to a classification position with customs

Even a modest percentage-point tariff difference (e.g. 2.5%) can translate into a substantial absolute duty demand on high-value equipment, so the classification question is worth resolving (including, where available, through an advance ruling) before, not after, import
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: confirmed: Supreme Court upheld classification of imported laser imagers (accessories to diagnostic machines, lacking independent diagnostic capability) under the residuary CTH 9033 rather than under 'other diagnostic instruments', resulting in a differential customs duty demand (Aug 2026, Carestream Health India matter)

topic_title: RERA Authority vs Adjudicating Officer: Who Can Actually Award You Interest on a Refund?
angle: A guide for homebuyers and developers on the division of functions within a state RERA structure between the Regulatory Authority (which decides substantive refund/compensation entitlement) and the Adjudicating Officer (who handles enforcement/execution), focused specifically on who has the power to fix interest.
key_points: A state RERA structure typically separates the Regulatory Authority's substantive adjudication function (deciding whether a refund, compensation or interest is owed, and at what rate) from the Adjudicating Officer's role, which is generally confined to quantifying and enforcing compensation claims under Sections 12, 14, 18 and 19

Courts have held that once the Regulatory Authority has already decided a homebuyer's entitlement to a refund, an Adjudicating Officer cannot independently layer on or re-fix an interest rate at the later enforcement/execution stage — interest, if payable, should be fixed as part of the Authority's substantive order

This matters practically because interest rates on RERA refunds vary significantly by state and by order (commonly linked to SBI's highest MCLR plus a margin, but not uniformly so) — a homebuyer should ensure the interest rate they expect is actually fixed in the Regulatory Authority's substantive order, not left to be decided later at enforcement

A developer facing an enforcement proceeding where the Adjudicating Officer has independently added an interest figure not present in the original Authority order has a specific, narrow ground to challenge that interest component (while the underlying refund direction itself may well stand)

Practical tip for homebuyers: if the original Authority order is silent or unclear on the interest rate, seek clarification or review from the Authority itself promptly, rather than waiting for the Adjudicating Officer to fix a rate at enforcement, since that may not survive challenge
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: confirmed: Madhya Pradesh High Court held a RERA Adjudicating Officer cannot independently award interest while enforcing a refund order once the Regulatory Authority had already decided refund entitlement, setting aside a separately-fixed 10% interest award (July 2026)

topic_title: Claiming You Own the Land Under a RERA Project? Why That Alone Won't Give You Standing at RERA
angle: A guide explaining why a person who is not an allottee — including someone asserting a competing ownership claim over the project land itself — generally lacks standing ('aggrieved person' status) to challenge a project's RERA registration, and must instead pursue a civil suit over title.
key_points: Section 31(1) of the RERA Act limits who can file a complaint to an 'aggrieved person' — a category tribunals have read as centred on allottees and others with a genuine stake in the project's performance, not merely anyone asserting an interest in the underlying land

A person who claims to be the true owner of the land on which a registered project sits, but who is not an allottee, has been held to lack standing to seek cancellation of that project's RERA registration on that basis alone — RERA registration proceeds on the developer's declared title and does not itself adjudicate competing ownership claims

Tribunals have consistently redirected such title disputes to the civil court as the proper forum, even where the land claimant alleges the registration itself was obtained by fraud — the fraud allegation does not convert a title dispute into a RERA-cognisable grievance

Practical point for a person disputing a developer's title: file (or continue) the civil suit over title promptly rather than routing the dispute through a RERA complaint, since the RERA forum is likely to decline jurisdiction regardless of how the claim is framed

This sits alongside, and should be read together with, the broader point that RERA registration is not a judicial finding of clear title — already covered in the site's existing guidance on protecting a well-known brand... [cross-reference the site's existing 'RERA cannot decide disputed questions of title' coverage]
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: confirmed: Telangana Real Estate Appellate Tribunal dismissed an appeal by land claimants seeking cancellation of the 'Aparna Sunstone' project's registration, holding they were not 'aggrieved persons' under Section 31(1) absent allottee status, and that their title claim belonged before a civil court (June 2026)

topic_title: CIRP Deadline Passed Without a Resolution Plan? Why Liquidation Follows Automatically
angle: A guide for creditors, resolution professionals and corporate debtors on what actually happens when a CIRP's statutory timeline expires without an approved resolution plan, explaining why Section 33(1)(a)'s liquidation consequence is treated as automatic rather than something the Committee of Creditors can vote to avoid.
key_points: If the CIRP period (including any approved extension) lapses without a resolution plan approved under Section 30(6), Section 33(1)(a) of the IBC requires the Adjudicating Authority to order liquidation — tribunals have treated this as an automatic statutory consequence of the deadline passing, not a discretionary outcome

A failed or deadlocked Committee of Creditors vote on a separate proposal (whether for a further extension or for liquidation itself) does not change this outcome — once the deadline has actually passed without a plan, the liquidation consequence attaches regardless of how, or whether, the CoC voted on liquidation as a distinct resolution

Expressions of interest or draft resolution plans received only after the CIRP period has already expired cannot revive the process or forestall liquidation — timing relative to the statutory deadline, not the existence of a late-arriving interested party, is what matters

Practical implication for a Committee of Creditors nearing a CIRP deadline: securing a valid extension (where the statutory conditions for one are met) before the deadline passes is the only way to avoid the automatic liquidation consequence — a vote taken after the deadline has already lapsed is too late regardless of its outcome

This is distinct from, and should not be confused with, a CoC's voluntary decision to recommend liquidation before the deadline (a Section 33(2) route), which does involve a CoC vote and commercial-wisdom considerations
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: confirmed: NCLAT held that once a CIRP period lapses without an approved resolution plan or a valid extension, Section 33(1)(a)'s liquidation consequence is automatically attracted, and a failed CoC vote on a separate liquidation proposal (or late expressions of interest) is irrelevant to that outcome (Oct 2026, Syska E-Retails matter)

topic_title: Sections 230-232 Scheme of Arrangement: What Actually Happens Between the First and Second NCLT Motion
angle: A practical guide for companies planning a merger, demerger or other scheme of arrangement under Sections 230-232 of the Companies Act, explaining the two-stage NCLT process — the first motion (convening meetings) and the second motion (sanction) — and what happens procedurally in between.
key_points: A scheme of arrangement under Sections 230-232 generally proceeds in two NCLT stages: a first-motion petition seeking directions to convene meetings of the relevant classes of shareholders/creditors (or dispensation of such meetings where consent is already obtained), followed by a second-motion petition seeking the Tribunal's sanction of the scheme itself

Between the two motions, the company must actually hold (or formally dispense with) the directed meetings, obtain the requisite majority approval from each class, and address any objections or regulatory observations (e.g. from the Registrar of Companies, Income Tax authorities, or sectoral regulators) raised in response to notice of the scheme

The gap between first-motion admission and the second-motion hearing can be substantial — commonly several weeks to a few months — depending on how quickly meetings are convened and regulatory responses are received, so companies should not treat first-motion admission as a signal the scheme is close to final sanction

A scheme's effective date and the transfer of assets/liabilities contemplated by it generally only crystallise upon the second-motion sanction order (and compliance with any further filing requirements), not upon first-motion admission — contracts and disclosures referencing the scheme should be drafted with this timing in mind
This is a practical companion to the site's existing guidance on demerger structuring, focused specifically on the NCLT procedural timeline rather than the substantive structuring choices
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: confirmed: NCLT Mumbai admitted the first-motion petition for the Larsen & Toubro / L&T Realty Properties scheme of arrangement on 18 August 2026, with the main (second-motion) hearing fixed for 6 October 2026 — illustrating a roughly six-week-plus gap between the two stages in that matter (2026)

topic_title: Can an Oppression and Mismanagement Petition Be Sent to Arbitration? The 'Dressed Up' Petition Test
angle: A narrow companion guide (distinct from the site's existing filing-procedure guide to oppression and mismanagement petitions) focused specifically on when a company dispute that looks like oppression/mismanagement can instead be pushed into arbitration under an arbitration clause in the company's shareholders' or partnership agreement.
key_points: Genuine oppression and mismanagement claims under Sections 241-242 of the Companies Act are generally treated as not arbitrable, since they invoke the NCLT's special statutory powers (akin to in rem relief) that an arbitral tribunal does not possess

Courts have nonetheless held that a petition merely 'dressed up' as oppression/mismanagement to sidestep an otherwise-applicable arbitration clause, or filed in a vexatious or mala fide manner, will not succeed in avoiding arbitration — the substance of the dispute, not its label, controls

Relevant factors courts weigh include whether the relief actually sought could equally be obtained through arbitration (e.g. a pure valuation/buy-out dispute between shareholders bound by a shareholders' agreement with an arbitration clause) versus relief that only the NCLT's statutory powers can provide (e.g. altering the company's management structure itself)

Where a related oppression/mismanagement-type dispute has already been pending before the NCLT/erstwhile CLB for a significant period with interim orders in place, a court has held this can itself render a parallel arbitration agreement inoperative for that dispute, rather than compelling arbitration late in the day

Practical point for drafting shareholders' agreements: if parties want disputes between themselves to go to arbitration, the agreement should address as specifically as possible which categories of dispute are intended for arbitration versus reserved for the NCLT's statutory jurisdiction, since ambiguity invites exactly this 'dressed up' characterisation fight
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: confirmed: Bombay High Court (Rakesh Malhotra v. Rajinder Kumar Malhotra line of authority) has held oppression/mismanagement claims are generally non-arbitrable but a petition merely dressed up to avoid arbitration, or vexatious/mala fide, will not succeed in avoiding it

note: the Delhi HC Vikram Bakshi v. McDonald's India authority on an arbitration agreement becoming inoperative due to a long-pending CLB proceeding should be verified for its current date/citation before publication, as the exact year was not confirmed in research

topic_title: Using Contract Staff? Why You (Not Just the Contractor) May Owe ESI Contributions
angle: A compliance guide for businesses engaging workers through a contractor/staffing agency, on why the principal employer commonly remains liable for ESI contributions on those workers, and the practical steps to manage that exposure.
key_points: Courts have held that routing workers through a contractor does not, by itself, shift ESI contribution liability away from the principal employer — the principal employer (the business where the work is actually performed) remains liable for ESI contributions on contract workers engaged at its premises or in its business

This mirrors a long-running, partly unsettled debate on the equivalent question under the EPF scheme, where some High Courts have held a contractor with its own independent PF code relieves the principal employer, while others (and EPFO's own 2017 circular) have taken the position that the principal employer retains overall compliance responsibility

Practical risk management steps for a principal employer: verify the contractor's actual ESI/EPF registration and contribution compliance before and during the engagement (not just at onboarding), retain documentary proof of the contractor's periodic compliance, and build indemnity/compliance-certification clauses into the contractor agreement

A principal employer that simply assumes the contractor's independent registration absolves it of liability risks a direct ESI demand against itself if the contractor's compliance turns out to be deficient — the statutory liability analysis does not depend on what the commercial contract between principal and contractor says about who is supposed to pay

This is distinct from, but should be read alongside, the general principal-employer-liability-for-contract-labour-wages guidance already on the site, since ESI/EPF statutory contribution liability and ordinary wage liability are governed by different statutory schemes with their own tests
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: confirmed: Calcutta High Court dismissed a writ challenging ESI authorities' determination of a principal employer's contribution liability for contract-engaged workers (2026, Height Insurance Services matter)
note: the EPF-side case law conflict (Madras HC vs Delhi HC/BHEL line) should be presented as genuinely unsettled, not resolved, and distinguished clearly from the more settled ESI position

topic_title: NHAI Withdrew Your Premium Deferment Facility for Default — What a Highway Concessionaire Can and Cannot Recover
angle: A guide for BOT highway concessionaires on how NHAI's premium-deferment relief works, what triggers its withdrawal for default, and what a concessionaire realistically can argue for in arbitration once withdrawn (illustrated by the Rs 1,202 crore Tumkur-Chitradurga/IRB award) — distinct from the existing queued guides on force-majeure extensions and toll revenue-loss claims, which deal with different stages of a concession dispute.
key_points: What the premium-deferment facility is: NHAI's relief mechanism letting a concessionaire defer part of its annual premium obligation under the concession agreement, rather than a waiver
Why NHAI withdraws it: repeated default on deferred premium payments is the trigger seen in reported cases, not a single missed instalment
What NHAI can counterclaim once withdrawn: full deferred premium arrears plus accrued interest, and related dues like unpaid revenue-share from ancillary structures (e.g., bypass revenue)

What a concessionaire's defence usually looks like: seeking restoration of the deferment and/or arguing force majeure or changed circumstances justified the default — and why tribunals have been reluctant to let this override a validly exercised contractual withdrawal

Procedural point: in the IRB case the tribunal left the exact computation to NHAI within a fixed window, with payment due afterward — illustrating how these awards are often structured as a declaration plus a computation mechanism rather than a fixed lump sum

Practical drafting/negotiation takeaway: the importance of documenting deferment requests and NHAI's responses contemporaneously, since the dispute often turns on whether deferment was validly sought/granted in the first place
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: confirmed: NHAI withdrew IRB Tumkur Chitradurga Tollway's premium deferment facility in August 2019 after repeated defaults (Construction World, Swarajya Mag, June/July 2026 reporting)

confirmed: arbitral tribunal (non-unanimous) awarded NHAI roughly Rs 1,202 crore on its counterclaims by award dated 25 June 2026, with computation to follow within 12 weeks and payment within a further 12 weeks (IRB InvIT Fund's own exchange filing, via scanx.trade)

fact to verify: the exact Model Concession Agreement clause number governing premium deferment and its withdrawal — not found in public reporting; pull from the MCA (2011 edition or the specific project's concession agreement) before drafting
fact to verify: whether IRB has filed or signalled a Section 34 challenge to this award — no source found either way as of this research

topic_title: How the RBI Actually Decides to Penalise a Bank or NBFC: The Section 47A Show-Cause Process Explained
angle: A practical guide for banks' and NBFCs' compliance and legal teams on the procedural stages between an RBI inspection finding and a published monetary penalty order — what to expect at each stage and where a regulated entity can meaningfully push back — illustrated by RBI's August 2026 batch of orders against IndusInd Bank, Northern Arc Capital, Muthoot MCred and Fusion Finance.
key_points: The statutory basis: Section 47A(1)(c) read with Sections 46(4)(i) and 56 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 for banks (co-operative banks draw on Section 51(1) for certain contraventions); a parallel penalty power exists under the RBI Act, 1934 for NBFCs

Stage 1 — statutory inspection: triggered by RBI's (or, for rural/co-operative banks, NABARD's) periodic inspection, assessed as of a specific financial-position date, not the date of the eventual order
Stage 2 — show-cause notice: RBI sets out the specific directions allegedly contravened and calls on the entity to show cause why a penalty should not be imposed

Stage 3 — reply and personal hearing: the entity's written reply is considered along with oral submissions at a personal hearing where one is sought; this is the real opportunity to narrow which charges are 'sustained'
Stage 4 — order: RBI records which charges it sustains (some can be dropped at this stage) and fixes the penalty amount per contravention, then publishes a press release/order

What the order deliberately does NOT decide: RBI's standard disclaimer that the penalty is based on regulatory compliance deficiencies only and doesn't pronounce on the validity of any transaction or agreement with customers — important for entities facing parallel civil claims

Typical penalty drivers seen across smaller NBFC orders: KYC risk-categorisation review lapses, NPA-to-standard account upgrades without full recovery, and inaccurate/incomplete complaint disclosures or failure to auto-escalate to the internal ombudsman
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: confirmed: RBI order dated 14 August 2026 fined IndusInd Bank Rs 59.20 lakh under Section 47A(1)(c) read with Section 46(4)(i) of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, based on an inspection as of 31 March 2025 (RBI's own press release)

confirmed: same batch (mid-August 2026) fined Northern Arc Capital Rs 6.20 lakh, Muthoot MCred Rs 3.10 lakh and Fusion Finance Rs 2.70 lakh (Moneylife, Hellobanker reporting corroborating RBI's releases)

fact to verify: the precise RBI Act, 1934 provision(s) under which the three NBFC penalties were formally issued (press coverage describes the conduct but not the exact section numbers for NBFCs specifically) — confirm from the individual RBI press releases/orders before publishing

fact to verify: whether a personal hearing was actually availed of in each of these four cases, or only offered — RBI's standard language covers both possibilities and the press reports don't distinguish

topic_title: Composer's Tune vs Producer's Recording: Why Two Different Copyrights Live Inside Every Old Film Song
angle: A guide for composers, producers, music labels and anyone re-recording or sampling an older Indian film song on the separate bundles of copyright in (a) the underlying musical work (the tune) and (b) the sound recording and lyrics, and why a licence from one rights-holder does not clear the other — illustrated by the Ilaiyaraaja/Saregama dispute over 'En Iniya Pon Nilave', distinct from the queued blog topics on patent revocation and GI disputes, which concern different IP regimes entirely.
key_points: The Copyright Act, 1957 treats the musical work (composition/tune), the literary work (lyrics) and the sound recording as three distinct 'works', each separately protectable and separately assignable

A film producer typically acquires the sound recording copyright (and often the lyrics) from the original producer/label by assignment, while the composer can retain rights only in the underlying musical work if the assignment did not cover it

Why this matters for a 'recreation': re-recording a song note-for-note with new vocals can still infringe the original sound recording copyright even with the composer's blessing, because the original recording's arrangement, performance and production are their own protected work

What a licensee actually needs to clear before using/recreating an old song: the musical work licence AND the sound recording licence AND the lyrics licence, potentially from three different rights-holders

Court review of 'prima facie' findings: how an interim/review-stage finding on who owns what differs from a final adjudication, and why a Supreme Court declining to interfere at the SLP stage is not the same as finally settling the ownership question

Practical checklist for producers commissioning a 'recreated' version of an older song: trace the chain of assignment for each of the three works separately before relying on any single party's licence
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: confirmed: Delhi High Court Division Bench held Ilaiyaraaja retains rights only in the musical work/tune of 'En Iniya Pon Nilave' (Moodu Pani, 1980), while Saregama India holds the sound recording and lyrics copyright by assignment from the original producer (LiveLaw, Bar & Bench, Deccan Chronicle, October 2026 reporting)
confirmed: Supreme Court (Justices Pardiwala and Vinod Chandran) declined to interfere with the High Court ruling around 1 October 2026, while characterising the High Court's findings as prima facie

fact to verify: the exact statutory provisions (Sections 13, 17, 18 of the Copyright Act, 1957) governing the three-way split should be pulled directly from the Act when drafting, rather than relied on from secondary news summaries

topic_title: Builder Handed Over Your Flat Without an Occupation Certificate? Why That's an Ongoing, Compensable Deficiency
angle: A guide for flat purchasers and housing societies on why possession handed over without a valid Occupation Certificate is treated as a continuing deficiency in service (not a one-time, time-barred default), what compensation and directions a consumer forum can order, and how a builder's attempt to blame the owners' own alterations is tested against actual evidence — illustrated by the NCDRC's Raja Construction/Santacruz ruling, distinct from the queued garnishee-order and medical-negligence consumer guides.
key_points: Why an OC matters beyond paperwork: occupancy without a valid OC can expose residents to civic-authority action (water/electricity connection risk, demolition exposure for unauthorised construction) quite apart from the consumer-law consequence

'Continuing deficiency' doctrine: because the builder's obligation to obtain and furnish the OC persists until actually fulfilled, the limitation period for a consumer complaint does not simply run from the date of possession — it keeps the claim alive for years

What triggers judicial skepticism of a builder's defence: an RTI-sourced comparison between sanctioned building plans and as-built construction is a powerful evidentiary tool buyers/societies can use themselves

Relief a consumer forum can order beyond a lump sum: a time-bound direction to actually obtain and hand over the OC (not just pay compensation and walk away), plus litigation costs and interest for delay in payment

Burden of proof point: a builder blaming the flat owners' own unauthorised alterations for an OC shortfall must actually prove that causal link — a bare assertion is not enough once deviation from sanctioned plans is otherwise shown
Practical steps for a housing society before litigating: file an RTI for the sanctioned plan and any OC-related correspondence early, since this becomes the evidentiary backbone of the claim
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: confirmed: NCDRC ordered Raja Construction Company to pay Rs. 6 crore to Tirupati Devi Co-operative Housing Society (Santacruz, Mumbai) for handing over possession without an OC and building beyond sanctioned plans, with payment due in three months and 8% interest on delay (LiveLaw, FreePressJournal, Moneylife, reported August 2026)

fact to verify: the precise 'continuing deficiency' limitation reasoning should be cross-checked against the Consumer Protection Act, 2019's own limitation provision (Section 69, two years from the date of cause of action) and existing NCDRC/Supreme Court precedent on when that cause of action is treated as recurring, rather than assumed from this one case

topic_title: Your Demerger Got NCLT Sanction — Why the Income Tax Department Can Still Come After It
angle: A guide for companies and their tax/legal teams on why an NCLT sanction order under Sections 230-232 of the Companies Act routinely preserves the Income Tax Department's right to examine or recover tax on the transaction, what that means practically for post-demerger tax exposure, and how it differs from the separate first/second-motion procedural guide already queued on this branch.
key_points: Why NCLT sanction is not a tax clearance: the Tribunal's jurisdiction under Sections 230-232 is about corporate/creditor/shareholder approval of the arrangement, not an assessment of its tax consequences — Regional Director objections routinely result in an explicit carve-out preserving Revenue's independent right to assess

What 'preserving the Income Tax Department's rights' actually means in practice: the demerged/resulting companies can still face reassessment, demand, or recovery proceedings tied to the scheme after sanction, and the sanction order itself cannot be cited to foreclose that

Typical undertakings a Regional Director extracts before recommending sanction: compliance with the Companies Act, tax laws, FEMA, and protection of creditors' and employees' interests — illustrated by the JSW Energy/GE Power India demerger sanction

Appointed date vs effective date mechanics: why a scheme's tax treatment often turns on the appointed date (which can be well before the sanction order) even though the scheme is not 'effective' until conditions precedent (including certified copy filing) are met

Share-exchange ratio disclosure and shareholder/creditor approval thresholds that evidence a scheme's bona fides, which both the Tribunal and (separately) tax authorities may scrutinise in their own proceedings

Practical drafting takeaway: build in indemnity/cost-sharing clauses between demerged and resulting companies for tax liabilities that crystallise after sanction, since the sanction order will not insulate either company from the Revenue's separate claim
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: confirmed: NCLT Mumbai Bench sanctioned the GE Power India/JSW Energy demerger on 1 October 2026 on condition of compliance undertakings, and expressly preserved the Income Tax Department's right to examine or recover tax on the transaction (LiveLawBiz, Sahi, Multibagg, October 2026 reporting)

confirmed: appointed date for that scheme is 1 July 2025, with a 10:139 JSW Energy-to-GE Power India share exchange ratio, approved by ~99.99% of valid shareholder votes and 85 of 86 unsecured creditors

fact to verify: the specific Income Tax Act provisions typically invoked by Revenue to reopen or examine a sanctioned scheme (e.g., Section 47 exemption conditions for demergers, or reassessment powers) should be confirmed against the Act before publishing, rather than left generic

topic_title: FSSAI Called Your Product 'Unsafe' — Not Just 'Substandard'. Here's Why That One Word Changes Everything
angle: A guide for food businesses on the legal difference between a food sample classified as 'unsafe' (Section 59, a criminal offence with escalating imprisonment depending on harm caused), 'substandard' (Section 51, a civil penalty for a quality-standards shortfall that does not render the food unsafe) and 'misbranded' (Section 52, a civil penalty for labelling/presentation defects) under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 — distinct from the already-queued guide on the scope of a batch-specific recall finding.
key_points: Section 59 (unsafe food): a criminal offence; penalties scale from up to 6 months' imprisonment and a fine up to Rs. 1 lakh where there is no injury, up to a minimum 7 years' (up to life) imprisonment and a minimum Rs. 10 lakh fine where the unsafe food causes death

Section 51 (substandard food): a civil, adjudication-officer-level penalty of up to Rs. 5 lakh for food that fails prescribed quality standards without being rendered unsafe — a materially lower-stakes finding than 'unsafe'
Section 52 (misbranded food): a civil penalty of up to Rs. 3 lakh for labelling, packaging or presentation defects, with the adjudicating officer also able to order corrective action or destruction

Why the same lab report can trigger more than one classification simultaneously for different defects found in a single sample, and why a business should scrutinise exactly which finding (and which statutory section) a notice actually invokes

The appeal path and what's realistically arguable: disputing the testing methodology (e.g., whether an additive's naturally occurring baseline was netted out before comparing to the permissible limit) is a recurring, fact-intensive defence seen in 'unsafe' findings over additive/contaminant levels

Practical compliance takeaway for a multi-outlet brand: an 'unsafe' finding against one retail sample is legally confined to that batch/sample, not an automatic finding against the brand's entire product line nationally — but the business still needs a documented, fast response given the criminal exposure
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: confirmed: FSSAI declared a Nestlé low-fat dairy whitener sample from The Lalit hotel, New Delhi, both 'unsafe' and 'substandard' on 3 October 2026, with Nestlé disputing the lab's phosphorus-measurement methodology (Khaleej Times/Reuters, Deccan Chronicle, Business Today, October 2026)

confirmed via Supreme Court case law reference (desikaanoon.in summary of SC ruling that Section 59 FSSA overrides Sections 272-273 IPC, and that substandard food cannot simultaneously be unsafe food under the statutory definitions) that the three categories are legally distinct and carry different consequences

fact to verify: the exact current fine/imprisonment figures under Sections 51, 52 and 59 should be confirmed against the current text of the FSS Act, 2006 (as amended) before publishing, since the research for this topic relied on secondary summaries for the figures

topic_title: Your Corporate Guarantee Has a Stamping Defect — Does That Kill Your Financial Creditor Status in Insolvency?
angle: A guide for lenders relying on corporate guarantees in an insolvency proceeding on why defects like insufficient stamping are 'curable' and do not defeat financial creditor status under Section 5(8) of the IBC, how this interacts with allegations that the guarantee itself was fraudulently executed, and what it means for getting onto (or being kept off) the Committee of Creditors — distinct from the already-queued guides on guarantee caps/interest and letter of comfort vs bank guarantee.
key_points: Why a corporate guarantee is 'financial debt' under Section 5(8) of the IBC: liability for repayment of money borrowed by another, guaranteed by the corporate debtor, falls within the definition regardless of whether the guarantor itself borrowed anything

The 'curable defect' principle: insufficient stamp duty on the guarantee instrument does not render it void — it can be cured (including after execution), so a lender's claim cannot be rejected on that ground alone, per SBI Consortium v. Doha Bank (2026 INSC 423) reiterating China Development Bank v. Doha Bank (2025) 7 SCC 729

Distinguishing a stamping defect from a fraud allegation: a bare allegation that the guarantee was executed when the guarantor was already in default, or was otherwise improperly obtained, requires actual proof — it is not a self-proving objection that defeats the claim automatically

What's at stake practically: exclusion from the Committee of Creditors strips a lender of voting rights over the resolution plan, so a guarantee-based claim's admission (or rejection) has outsized consequences beyond the guarantee amount itself

Standard of review when a lender challenges NCLT/NCLAT findings rejecting its guarantee claim: the Supreme Court will intervene where concurrent findings are 'perverse and legally unsustainable', a high bar but not an insurmountable one

Practical drafting/diligence takeaway for lenders taking corporate guarantees: cure any stamping shortfall promptly when discovered rather than assuming it is immaterial, since the curable-defect principle removes the risk but not the friction/delay of having to cure it mid-dispute
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: confirmed: Supreme Court in State Bank of India & Ors. v. Doha Bank Q.P.S.C. & Anr. (2026 INSC 423, decided 28 April 2026) held corporate guarantee liability is financial debt under Section 5(8) IBC and that stamping defects are curable and do not void the instrument (Verdictum, Mondaq, IndiaLaw reporting)

fact to verify: the precise holding and citation of China Development Bank v. Doha Bank Q.P.S.C. (2025) 7 SCC 729 should be pulled from the actual law report rather than relied on via secondary commentary describing it as reiterated

topic_title: A Foreign Court Awarded Damages Against Your Indian Company — Can FEMA or RBI Rules Cap What You Actually Pay?
angle: A guide for Indian companies that raised RBI-approved foreign-currency debt (ECBs, FCCBs) on why a foreign court's damages decree for breach of the underlying instrument is enforced in India at its full adjudicated value, and is not capped or curtailed by the FEMA/RBI pricing or remittance ceilings that governed the original borrowing — distinct from the queued guides on NRI property FEMA rules and RBI's digital lending directions.
key_points: The core holding: damages a competent court (Indian or foreign) awards for breach of contract are not subject to FEMA or RBI ceilings merely because the underlying instrument (e.g., an FCCB) was itself RBI-approved and FEMA-governed at issuance

Why Section 13 of the CPC's narrow exceptions to foreign-judgment conclusiveness (fraud, lack of jurisdiction, violation of Indian law's fundamental principles, etc.) do not include 'the award exceeds what RBI pricing guidelines would have allowed'

What this means for ECB/FCCB default scenarios: a lender is not limited to the contractually agreed redemption premium or coupon if a foreign court, applying the governing law of the instrument, awards a different (often higher) damages figure for breach

The appeal landscape: an execution-stage ruling allowing enforcement is itself appealable to a Division Bench, so 'enforcement allowed' at the single-judge execution stage is not necessarily final — track the appeal before treating a ruling as settled

Practical guidance for Indian borrowers negotiating foreign-law-governed debt instruments: build protective caps or liquidated-damages clauses into the loan/bond documentation itself if a FEMA-ceiling-style limit is commercially desired, since the ceiling will not be read into the contract by an Indian court at the enforcement stage
Costs consequence of resisting enforcement on a FEMA/RBI objection that doesn't fit within Section 13 CPC: courts have been willing to dismiss such objections with costs against the objecting company
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: confirmed: Delhi High Court (Justice Amit Bansal) in Peter Beck und Partner Vermögensverwaltung GmbH v. Prakash Industries Ltd. (2026:DHC:1547, February 2026) allowed enforcement of an England & Wales Commercial Court decree despite FEMA/RBI objections, dismissing the objections with Rs. 1 lakh costs (Verdictum, LiveLawBiz, Mondaq reporting)
confirmed: an appeal against this ruling is pending before the Delhi High Court Division Bench as of the research date — the topic should note the ruling is not yet final at the appellate level

fact to verify: the exact FCCB terms (coupon rate vs. Early Redemption Amount figures) differ between secondary sources and should be pulled from the English judgment or the execution petition record rather than estimated

topic_title: Already Filed to Enforce Your Foreign Arbitral Award in India? You May Still Be Able to Get Section 9 Interim Relief
angle: A guide for parties holding a foreign arbitral award on why filing a Part II petition for recognition and enforcement under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act does not, by itself, shut off the separate option of seeking interim relief under Section 9 to protect against asset dissipation while that petition is pending — distinct from the queued guides on enforcing foreign awards generally and on emergency arbitrators.
key_points: The two-stage character of a Part II enforcement petition: it is first a proceeding on recognition and enforceability under Sections 48-49, and only becomes an execution proceeding once the court records satisfaction that the award is enforceable — Section 9 jurisdiction continues through that first stage

Why this matters practically: an award-debtor often has every incentive to dissipate assets while a recognition petition is pending, since enforcement/execution hasn't formally started — Section 9 lets the award-creditor freeze that risk in the interim
How to actually use this: a party can file a 'rolled-up' application combining the Part II enforcement petition with a Section 9 request, rather than waiting for recognition to be decided first

The open question flagged by commentators: whether Section 9 relief remains available once the award has actually been recognised as a decree and the matter has moved into execution — High Courts are described as still divided, so don't assume this extends indefinitely

Contrast with a party resisting enforcement: a non-signatory or genuinely disputing third party cannot use Section 9 to 'resurrect' liability once an enforcement court has already rejected enforcement against them — the relief runs with recognition, not against it

Practical drafting/strategy takeaway for award-creditors: identify and plead the specific assets at dissipation risk when seeking Section 9 relief alongside a Part II petition, since the relief is framed as protective, not a freestanding attachment power
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: confirmed: Bombay High Court (Justice Somasekhar Sundaresan) in Österreichischer Lloyd Seereederei (Cyprus) Ltd. v. Victore Ships Pvt. Ltd. (Commercial Arbitration Petition No. 398 of 2025, decided 10 March 2026) held Section 9 relief available even after a Part II enforcement petition is filed, granting relief on an award of roughly USD 269,105.08 (Verdictum, Conventus Law, JSA, Cyril Amarchand reporting)

fact to verify: whether any subsequent 2026 ruling has resolved the 'divided High Courts' question on Section 9 availability post-recognition/at the execution stage — the research found this flagged as open but did not locate a resolving judgment, so the blog draft should state it as unsettled rather than assume a resolution

topic_title: A Competitor's Pesticide Registration Looks Shaky — Can You Actually Get It Cancelled?
angle: A guide for agrochemical manufacturers on how to challenge a rival's registration certificate under Section 9(3) of the Insecticides Act, 1968 by letters patent appeal/writ where the Registration Committee approved it on an evidentiary gap (such as a mismatch between the manufacturer named at the trial-import stage and the one later approved for commercial registration), illustrated by Dhanuka Agritech's successful challenge to Crystal Crop Protection's Halosulfuron Methyl registration — distinct from the already-published compliance guide aimed at the registrant/dealer side.
key_points: Standing: a competing registered manufacturer of the same or a substitutable active ingredient has standing to challenge a rival's Section 9(3) registration grant, since the grant directly affects its competitive position in that market

The specific evidentiary gap that succeeded in the Dhanuka/Crystal Crop case: the 2016 commercial registration application named a manufacturer that had only received its own (temporary) registration to produce the active ingredient in October 2018 — after the relevant approval point — leaving no evidentiary basis for the Committee's 2016 approval

Why 'manifestly illegal' is the standard courts apply to a Registration Committee's technical/scientific approval, and what kind of gap in the record (as opposed to a mere disagreement with the Committee's judgment) meets that bar

The procedural route: appeal under Section 10 of the Act to the government first where available, versus a writ/letters patent appeal challenging the underlying Registration Committee decision directly — and why getting the route wrong can cost years

What quashing the registration actually stops: the registrant can no longer import the underlying technical-grade material or manufacture the formulated product domestically under that registration, a serious commercial disruption that creates real incentive to litigate hard on both sides

Practical diligence takeaway for a manufacturer bringing or defending such a challenge: trace the chain of authorisations for the named overseas/domestic manufacturer as of the date of each relevant application, since timing gaps in that chain are exactly where these challenges succeed or fail
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: confirmed: Delhi High Court Division Bench (Justices C. Hari Shankar and Om Prakash Shukla) quashed Crystal Crop Protection's Halosulfuron Methyl registration in Dhanuka Agritech Ltd. v. Union of India & Ors. (LPA 215/2023, judgment dated 29 May 2026), finding the Registration Committee had no evidence the named manufacturer (Jiangsu Agrochemicals) was authorised to produce the material at the relevant time (agrospectrumindia.com, caseon.in case record)

fact to verify: the exact text and scope of Section 10 of the Insecticides Act, 1968 (the statutory appeal route) versus when a direct writ/LPA challenge is available should be confirmed against the Act itself before publishing, since the research surfaced both routes being used in different reported cases without a clear rule distinguishing when each applies

topic_title: The Sale Agreement You Signed Doesn't Match What the Builder Filed With RERA — Does That Matter?
angle: A guide for homebuyers and developers on Rule 38 of the state RERA rules, which requires a developer to use the standard-form sale agreement it uploaded to the RERA portal at project registration, what counts as a 'material' deviation that triggers a false-information/suppression penalty under Section 60, and how this penalty is separate from (and additional to) whatever contractual relief the buyer separately obtains — illustrated by the Telangana REAT's Mehta & Modi Realty ruling, distinct from the queued guides on RERA forfeiture caps and the RERA/adjudicating-officer interest-power split.
key_points: What Rule 38 (and equivalent state rules) actually requires: the agreement for sale executed with individual buyers must follow the prescribed format, matching the draft uploaded to RERA at project registration, not a bespoke version the developer negotiates buyer-by-buyer

Why a materially different executed agreement is treated as 'false information' and 'suppression of material facts' under Section 60 of the RERA Act, a penalty distinct from — and additional to — any delay-interest or possession relief a buyer separately claims

The kind of deviations that have drawn penalties in reported cases: altered payment schedules, different delay-compensation terms, and clauses shifting statutory obligations (like who bears GST on delay interest) onto the buyer

What a buyer can do on discovering a mismatch: complain to the state RERA authority directly rather than treating it as a pure contract dispute, since the regulator can penalise the developer and set aside the offending clauses regardless of what the individually signed agreement says

Why 'the buyer signed it' is not a defence: RERA's project-registration-stage filing creates a baseline the developer cannot unilaterally depart from in individual contracts, so a signed deviation does not cure the Rule 38 violation

Collateral directions regulators have ordered alongside the penalty: barring a developer from passing on GST on delay interest, ordering dissolution of a developer-controlled 'welfare association', and requiring pending work to be completed before further handover — showing the remedy often goes well beyond the headline fine
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: confirmed: Telangana Real Estate Appellate Tribunal upheld an approximately Rs. 11 lakh penalty against Mehta & Modi Realty Kowkur LLP for a sale agreement materially different from its RERA-uploaded draft, under Rule 38 of the Telangana RERA Rules and Section 60 of the RERA Act (T.A. No. 45 of 2025, judgment dated 6 May 2026; LiveLawBiz, Mondaq reporting)

fact to verify: the exact rule number and text should be confirmed against each specific state's RERA rules when drafting for a non-Telangana audience, since the 'standard agreement format' requirement is typically a state-rule provision (not uniform central RERA Act text) and numbering can differ by state

topic_title: Suing an NBFC Over a Loan in Civil Court? Section 45QA of the RBI Act May Mean You're in the Wrong Forum Entirely
angle: A guide for lenders and borrowers on Section 45QA of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934 (read with Section 430 of the Companies Act, 2013), which gives the NCLT exclusive jurisdiction over certain disputes involving non-banking financial companies, when a dispute framed as an ordinary contractual claim can actually be barred from civil court on this ground, and why getting the forum wrong can mean losing years of litigation to a jurisdictional dismissal — illustrated by the Allahabad High Court's Shivam Traders ruling, distinct from the queued Order XXXVII summary-suit guide, which concerns a different recovery mechanism within civil court itself.
key_points: What Section 45QA actually covers: disputes falling within specific categories tied to RBI's regulatory jurisdiction over NBFCs (illustrated by a premature-loan-repayment dispute between two NBFCs in the reported case), read together with Section 430 of the Companies Act, which bars civil courts from entertaining matters the NCLT is empowered to decide

Why framing a claim as a 'simple contract dispute' does not avoid the bar: if the underlying subject matter falls within the NCLT's statutory domain under these provisions, a civil court lacks jurisdiction regardless of how the plaint is drafted

The practical risk: a civil suit proceeding for years before the jurisdictional objection is raised (or noticed by the court itself) can be dismissed at that late stage, as happened in the reported case — so forum should be checked at the drafting stage, not left to be raised defensively

How this interacts with co-lending arrangements between banks and NBFCs: a dispute arising from a co-lending arrangement governed by RBI's 2025 Co-Lending Directions may raise the same forum question, since RBI-regulated NBFC conduct is the common thread
What relief is actually available at the NCLT for this kind of dispute, and how that differs procedurally from a civil suit (timelines, appeal route to NCLAT rather than a civil appellate hierarchy)

Practical drafting takeaway: before filing (or defending) a suit involving an NBFC's lending conduct, check whether the specific dispute category falls within Section 45QA's scope — and if unsure, consider filing protectively before the NCLT or seeking an early jurisdictional ruling rather than litigating the merits for years first
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: confirmed: Allahabad High Court (Justice Sandeep Jain) in Shivam Traders and Hire Purchase Pvt. Ltd. v. Madhusudan Vehicles Pvt. Ltd. (2026:AHC:67074, order dated 31 March 2026) held only the NCLT has jurisdiction over a premature-loan-repayment dispute under Section 45QA RBI Act read with Section 430 Companies Act, dismissing a Rs. 19.25 crore civil suit for lack of jurisdiction (Verdictum, LiveLawBiz reporting)

fact to verify: the precise scope of disputes Section 45QA covers (as opposed to ordinary civil claims against an NBFC that remain within civil court jurisdiction) should be confirmed against the statutory text and any appellate clarification, since the reported case is a single High Court ruling on one fact pattern (premature repayment) and should not be generalised to all NBFC disputes without that check

topic_title: Your Competitor Says Your Design Is Just a 'Mosaic' of Old Products — Why That Defence Usually Fails
angle: A guide for holders of a registered industrial design on why a defendant cannot defeat an infringement claim merely by showing that individual elements of its design each appear separately in different prior-art products, and what 'mosaicing' actually means as a prohibited style of argument — a post-registration enforcement topic distinct from the published guide on the design registration process itself, which does not cover infringement litigation defences.
key_points: What 'mosaicing of prior art' means: assembling bits and pieces from multiple different earlier designs, none of which individually shows the registered design as a whole, to argue the registered design lacks novelty or that the accused product merely copies 'old' elements

Why courts reject this at the interim stage: the test for infringement is visual similarity of the design AS A WHOLE to the registered design, not a feature-by-feature scavenger hunt through unrelated prior products

The role of an un-denied visual comparison: where a defendant's reply doesn't actually dispute that the two products look alike, a court can treat that silence as effectively conceding the prima facie case

What relief looks like at the interim stage: a defendant already selling the accused product is typically allowed to complete/clear existing sales but barred from further ones, often coupled with a sales-disclosure obligation (records filed by affidavit, sometimes in a sealed cover) so the eventual damages/accounts exercise has a real evidentiary base
Why a short registration history (a design registered only a year or two before the dispute) is not itself a weakness — there's no minimum 'vintage' requirement for a design to be forcefully enforced

Practical takeaway for a design holder: document and preserve the registration certificate and prosecution history early, since swift interim relief turns on a clean prima facie comparison, not a prolonged validity fight
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: confirmed: Delhi High Court (Justice Tushar Rao Gedela) granted Orient Electric an interim injunction against Crompton's 'Grace' ceiling fan on 14 May 2026, rejecting a 'mosaic of prior art designs' defence and holding visual similarity to Orient's registered 'AEON' design 'unmistakable' (LiveLawBiz, BananaIP, Maheshwari & Co. reporting)

fact to verify: the precise statutory basis for rejecting a mosaicing argument (interplay of Sections 4, 19 and 22 of the Designs Act, 2000, on novelty/originality and infringement) should be confirmed against the Act and any appellate ruling on this specific point before publishing, since the research relied on case reporting rather than a doctrinal treatise

topic_title: Bank Moved Your Loan's Interest to a 'Suspense Account' After NPA Classification — You Still Owe It
angle: A guide for borrowers and lenders on why interest a bank books in a separate suspense account after a loan is classified as a Non-Performing Asset remains part of the legally recoverable 'debt', and why a borrower cannot rely on the bank's internal accounting treatment to argue that interest has somehow been written off or excluded — illustrated by the Supreme Court's PNB v. Shree Jyoti Education Trust ruling, distinct from the published bank-fraud-classification RBI guide, which concerns a different classification (fraud reporting) rather than NPA interest accounting.
key_points: Why banks use a suspense account at all: standard prudential accounting practice stops accruing interest to the profit and loss account once a loan turns NPA, routing it instead to a suspense/memorandum account so the bank's books don't overstate income on a doubtful asset
The borrower's (losing) argument: that because the interest sits in a separate ledger head rather than the main loan account, it is somehow not 'real' debt or has been effectively waived

The statutory anchor for the opposite conclusion: Section 2(g) of the Recovery of Debts and Bankruptcy Act, 1993 defines 'debt' broadly to include any liability 'inclusive of interest' — the definition doesn't carve out interest parked in a suspense account
Why a DRT/DRAT recovery certificate computed with this interest included will survive a challenge based purely on the accounting-head argument

The 'can't pick and choose' principle: a borrower (or trust/trustee) cannot invoke one accounting figure at one stage of litigation and a different, lower figure at another stage to suit the argument being made at that moment

Practical takeaway for a borrower negotiating a settlement: don't assume a lower 'principal + visible interest' figure quoted informally reflects the bank's full legal claim — ask specifically whether suspense-account interest is included before treating any settlement number as final
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: confirmed: Supreme Court (2026 INSC 836, 12 August 2026) restored a DRAT recovery order of Rs. 54.90 lakh against a trust after Orissa HC had directed PNB to accept a lower ~Rs. 29.56 lakh settlement, holding suspense-account interest is part of recoverable debt under Section 2(g) RDB Act (Verdictum, LiveLaw, Outlook Money reporting)

fact to verify: the specific RBI prudential norms/circular provisions governing suspense-account treatment of NPA interest should be pulled from RBI's current Master Direction on income recognition and asset classification before publishing, since the research relied on case reporting of the practice rather than the underlying RBI circular text

topic_title: Does Running Your Own Power Lines Make You a 'Distribution Licensee'? The Electricity Act's Two-Part Test
angle: A guide for any large captive user of electricity (railways, ports, industrial estates, large campuses) with its own power distribution infrastructure on the two-part statutory test for whether that infrastructure makes the operator a 'deemed distribution licensee' under the Electricity Act, 2003 — and why that classification matters enormously for open-access surcharge liability — illustrated by the Supreme Court's Indian Railways ruling, distinct from the published guide on a distribution licensee's universal-service obligations, which assumes licensee status rather than addressing how that status is determined.
key_points: The twin test: 'distribution' under the Electricity Act requires BOTH (a) operating a distribution system AND (b) supplying electricity to third-party consumers within a specific area — satisfying only the first half doesn't qualify

Why a sector-specific statute authorising an entity to build/operate its own electrical infrastructure (illustrated by Section 11 of the Railways Act, 1989) does not, by itself, confer distribution-licensee status under the separate Electricity Act framework — the two statutes answer different questions

The practical stakes: a 'consumer' (not a deemed licensee) procuring power through open access is liable for cross-subsidy surcharge and additional surcharge, which a true distribution licensee supplying its own network of third-party consumers would not pay in the same way

Why 'self-consumption only' is fatal to a deemed-licensee claim: an entity that uses 100% of the electricity on its own distribution network for its own operations, with no third-party consumers on that network, fails the second half of the twin test categorically

How this plays out for large campus/estate operators (SEZs, industrial parks, large townships) running internal distribution networks: the same twin test applies, so an operator supplying tenants/third parties on its network is in a materially different position from one serving only its own operations

Practical takeaway: before relying on 'we built and run our own lines' as a basis to claim distribution-licensee status (and the surcharge exemptions that come with it), confirm whether the network actually supplies third-party consumers, not just the operator's own facilities
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: confirmed: Supreme Court (2026 INSC 464, 8 May 2026, Justices Dipankar Datta and Satish Chandra Sharma) held Indian Railways is not a deemed distribution licensee and must pay cross-subsidy/additional surcharge on open-access power procurement (Verdictum, Renewable Watch, JSA reporting)

fact to verify: the exact statutory provision establishing the twin test (reporting cites a 'third proviso' to Section 14 in one source and Section 143 in another) should be confirmed against the current text of the Electricity Act, 2003 before publishing

topic_title: NHAI Terminated Your Contract on Two Grounds — Winning on One in Court Doesn't Mean You've Won
angle: A guide for EPC/BOT contractors on why a termination notice citing multiple independent grounds requires a court challenge to actually address EACH ground, and why a High Court ruling that only engages with one of several grounds is vulnerable to a stay or reversal on appeal — illustrated by the Supreme Court's stay in NHAI v. Tata Projects, distinct from the queued guide on NHAI's premium-deferment withdrawal, which concerns a different stage of concession disputes (deferment relief, not a multi-ground termination notice).
key_points: Why authorities like NHAI often cite more than one ground in a termination notice: each ground is independently capable of justifying termination, so even if a contractor successfully challenges one, the termination can still stand on the other(s)

The litigation trap this creates for a contractor: winning a writ/arbitration challenge by focusing on the more easily disprovable ground (e.g., a timeline-completion default where delay-causation evidence favours the contractor) means little if the court record never actually engages with the second ground (e.g., a maintenance-of-existing-infrastructure default)

What a reviewing court (or the Supreme Court on appeal/SLP) will look for: whether the lower court's judgment contains any reasoning addressing each cited ground, not just the one the parties argued most vigorously

The 'practical impossibility' argument and its limits: a contractor arguing that maintaining old infrastructure while building new infrastructon the same stretch is impractical needs to actually make that argument and get a ruling on it — a court won't infer that ground was implicitly rejected just because the contractor won on the other ground

Why a stay (rather than a final reversal) is the likely outcome when an unaddressed ground is identified at the SLP stage: the Supreme Court in such cases often restores the parties' dispute to a live, contested status rather than deciding the unaddressed ground itself in the first instance

Practical takeaway for drafting a Section 34/writ challenge to a multi-ground termination: structure the pleading to address every ground cited in the notice individually, even the one that looks weaker, so the resulting judgment can't be picked apart for an unaddressed point later
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: confirmed: Supreme Court (Justices J.B. Pardiwala and K. Vinod Chandran) stayed the Allahabad High Court's judgment quashing NHAI's termination of Tata Projects' Rs. 940.68 crore EPC contract on 31 August 2026, after the Solicitor General argued the High Court had not addressed NHAI's second termination ground (Foxmandal, LiveLaw, LiveLawBiz reporting)

fact to verify: the current status/outcome of the underlying dispute following the stay (whether the parties reached a resolution as the Supreme Court directed, or the matter proceeded to further hearing) was not resolved by this research and should be checked before publishing, since the stay order itself does not finally decide the termination's validity

topic_title: The Regional Director Flagged an Issue in Your Merger Scheme — Here's How Companies Actually Clear It
angle: A guide for companies navigating NCLT sanction of a Sections 230-232 merger/amalgamation scheme on how a Regional Director's specific objections (secured-creditor charges, pending tax proceedings, FEMA compliance, employee protections) typically get resolved in practice — through company undertakings addressed to those concerns, rather than independent adjudication by the Tribunal — distinct from the queued guide on the first/second NCLT motion procedure and the queued guide on the tax department's rights surviving a sanctioned demerger, which address different stages/aspects of the same broader process.
key_points: What a Regional Director's report actually is: a standard-practice filing in Section 230-232 proceedings flagging specific statutory compliance concerns for the Tribunal's attention before sanction, not an independent veto

Why 'undertaking' is the normal currency of resolution: rather than litigating whether secured-creditor charges are properly protected or whether pending tax proceedings are addressed, companies typically file written undertakings committing to specific compliance steps, which the Tribunal then relies on in granting sanction

topic_title: Can Your Employer Investigate a Sexual Harassment Complaint Through Its Normal Disciplinary Process? No.

Why 'the facts would come out the same either way' is not a defence: the POSH framework's procedural protections (the ICC's composition requirements, including an external member, confidentiality rules, and the complainant's specific rights during the inquiry) are not replicated in an ordinary departmental inquiry, so substituting one for the other is a procedural defect, not a harmless formality

What happens to action taken on the wrong inquiry's findings: a termination (or other disciplinary action) built on findings from an inquiry conducted outside the ICC/LCC framework is vulnerable to being quashed on that ground alone, regardless of how the underlying facts might have come out in a proper ICC inquiry

Practical guidance for an employer facing a sexual harassment complaint against an employee: route it to the ICC/LCC from the outset, even if a separate disciplinary concern also exists on overlapping facts — don't let a departmental inquiry get ahead of or substitute for the mandatory ICC process

What an employee facing termination on this basis can argue: that the inquiry body itself was not constituted or empowered under the POSH Act, which is a structural defect a court can address without needing to re-examine the underlying factual allegations

Where this leaves the underlying harassment allegation: quashing a termination for using the wrong inquiry body does not exonerate the employee on the merits — it typically means the employer must restart via the correct ICC/LCC process if it wishes to pursue the matter

Why this is a faster, lower-evidentiary-bar enforcement tool than a composition-based 'unsafe' or 'substandard' finding: FSSAI doesn't need to wait for or rely on lab test results to act on branding/naming/imagery alone

Why a defendant might be tempted to file an Order VII Rule 11 application late: it looks like a way to pause the clock by putting the suit's maintainability itself in question, rather than engaging on the merits within the deadline

Why that doesn't work once the deadline has already lapsed: a defendant may legitimately choose to seek rejection of the plaint BEFORE filing a written statement (i.e., within the 120 days), but can't use a late-filed Order VII Rule 11 application as a device to recover time already lost

What a defendant should actually do if there's a genuine Order VII Rule 11 ground: file it promptly, within the 120-day window, rather than waiting — timing the application correctly is itself part of using this defence properly

The interaction with other pending defences: a separate substantive defence (like an IBC moratorium argument) raised in a late Order VII Rule 11 application doesn't get a free pass either — it gets decided within that (already late) application on its own timeline, it doesn't retroactively excuse the written-statement delay

Practical takeaway for defence counsel: calendar the 120-day deadline as the single most important date in a commercial suit, and if a plaint-rejection argument exists, file it well within that window rather than treating it as a fallback option to be raised only if a written statement doesn't get filed in time

topic_title: When Can a Trade Association and Its Office-Bearers Be Penalised Under Competition Law?
angle: A practical guide for trade bodies, industry associations and their elected office-bearers on how Sections 3(3)(b) and 48 of the Competition Act, 2002 can make an association — and the individuals who ran it at the relevant time — personally liable for coordinating boycotts, price understandings or supply restrictions among members, using the CCI's 2026 action against agro-input dealer associations as the anchor example.
key_points: Section 3(3)(b) catches horizontal arrangements among competing members — including informal association resolutions or circulars — that limit or control production, supply, markets, technical development, investment or the provision of services, without needing a signed contract.

An association 'deciding' something at a general body meeting or through office-bearer communication can itself be treated as the anti-competitive agreement; CCI does not need to prove a formal written cartel pact.

Section 48 extends liability to individuals who were in charge of, and responsible for, the association's conduct of business at the time of the contravention — typically office-bearers such as president, general secretary or named spokespersons.

A named office-bearer has a statutory due-diligence defence: liability does not attach if the contravention occurred without their knowledge, or if they exercised all diligence to prevent it — this must be affirmatively pleaded and evidenced.

Remedies under Section 27 go beyond fines: CCI can issue cease-and-desist directions (27(a)) and, increasingly, non-monetary remedies such as mandated competition-compliance training for the association and its members (27(g)).
Penalties on associations and individual office-bearers are often modest in absolute terms, but the compliance burden, reputational consequences, and precedent value can be significant.

Practical compliance steps for associations: avoid discussing competitively sensitive topics (pricing, boycotts of specific channels or counterparties, output limits) at meetings; keep minutes that record antitrust caution; limit what office-bearers can commit the association to; adopt a written competition-compliance policy before a CCI reference ever arises.
